findings.trigger_invalidation: Cap is binding when a strategy's loss distribution shows realized tails beyond the modeled 99th percentile on frozen OOS, or when a negative-skew harvest strategy is not admitted through RiskGate without a tail-exposure cap.
findings.risk_geometry: Risk rule: tail-exposure cap per instrument, one exposure per (instrument, direction), heat cap; not an entry setup.
findings.quote: They made absolutely no allowance in the LTCM episode for the possibility of their not understanding markets and their methods being wrong.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 13 'Computing Instead of Thinking' (p. 189)
findings.notes: Case-study storytelling (LTCM), not a controlled test, hence NARRATIVE. In crypto perps leverage and liquidation cascades make negative-skew harvest strategies acutely dangerous; the crypto analogue mechanism is the deleveraging_cascade / carry_unwind family.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Black-swan crisis harvesting (long convexity)
findings.setup_summary: Portfolio-level strategy of being structurally long tail risk: accept small recurring losses while holding convexity that pays off in market breakdowns ('profiting from the black swans and the breakdown of the system'), the inverse of LTCM's book.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Cannot be expressed in a perps-only book without options/vol instruments; deferred pending venue expansion (crypto options) or a convexity-approximation design.
findings.risk_geometry: Small, repeated premium-like losses; payoff concentrated in rare breakdown events; requires long expiry and no stop that would cut the convex payoff.
findings.quote: I happen to specialize in profiting from the black swans and the breakdown of the system, and make bets against financial economists.
findings.notes: LOW applicability: V8 models Binance USDM perps only, and the canonical expression needs options or vol products. Recorded as a backlog family so the positive-skew preference survives as a screening criterion even though the tradable form is out of venue.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Outcome-independent execution protocol
findings.setup_summary: Execution and evaluation follow a pre-committed protocol that does not vary with the last outcome: the same rules run whether the last five episodes won or lost. Ancient evaluation judged heroes by actions, not results, and dignity is the execution of a behavior protocol independent of immediate circumstance.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Methodology principle, not a tradable setup; falsifiable only as process adherence (episode scores should record protocol compliance separately from outcome).
findings.risk_geometry: None.
findings.quote: dignity defined as the execution of a protocol of behavior that does not depend on the immediate circumstance
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 14 'Bacchus Abandons Antony' (p. 192)
findings.notes: Philosophical rationale for V8's deterministic rules, RiskGate admission and outcome-independent episode scoring: the system must not be re-tuned based on recent win/loss streaks.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: News-causality noise rejection
findings.setup_summary: Treat every news-headline explanation of a price move as noise unless the move exceeded its usual magnitude; never use journalistic causal attribution as a feature. Sub-significance moves (< usual daily move, e.g., 1.03 Dow points at 11,000) have no adducible cause, and single-cause attribution is invalid in a multivariate world without isolating factors and reaching a >=90% confidence level.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Methodology/design lesson: confirmed in V8 by the tape pipeline already excluding news text and wall-clock commentary from the decision path.
findings.risk_geometry: None.
findings.quote: the journalist claims to provide an explanation for something that amounts to perfect noise
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 11 'The Bloomberg Explanations' (p. 165); multivariate/causality requirement p. 166
findings.notes: Validates V8's determinism rule (no news feed, no wall clock in replay). 24/7 crypto commentary volume makes this guard more salient, not less.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Index-vs-component maximum bias
findings.setup_summary: When aggregating across instruments, the maximum of an average is less volatile than the average maximum: components do not peak together, so component drawdowns run far deeper than the index drawdown. Cross-instrument max-based features (e.g., each perp's distance from its own high) must not be read as index-level signal.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Statistical fact; applies whenever V8 features aggregate multiple instruments (currently single-instrument BTCUSDT).
findings.risk_geometry: None.
findings.quote: By a law of probability called distribution of the maximum of random variables, the maximum of an average is necessarily less volatile than the average maximum.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 11 opening (p. 163)
findings.notes: A mathematical property of maxima, hence falsifiable. Becomes actionable when V8 expands to cross_market feature groups or altcoin perps: index-level stats understate component tails.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Conditional probability updating
findings.setup_summary: Probability estimates must be conditional on the state actually reached: unconditional life expectancy at birth differs from conditional life expectancy given survival to age X. Applied to evaluation, a strategy that has survived N episodes has conditional properties different from its unconditional backtest properties; 'our operation has 1% mortality, so the 100th patient dies' is the fallacy to avoid.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Estimation rule: any registry/replication estimate must condition on the sample-selection state (survival to that sample size), else it embeds the unconditional/conditional confusion.
findings.risk_geometry: None.
findings.quote: What these journalists confuse is the unconditional and conditional life expectancy.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 11 opening (p. 164)
findings.notes: Basic probability logic (conditional vs unconditional), falsifiable. Guards the lab: replication estimates for a surviving expert version are conditional estimates and must be labeled as such, not pooled with unconditional statistics.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Stop hunting / post-breach momentum (Osler)
findings.setup_summary: Stops cluster at support/resistance and at round numbers near price. Once price pierces the level, the triggered sell (buy) stops push price further down (up) for a while; HFTs can also preemptively push price toward the level to ignite the cascade and cover. Falsifiable on BTCUSDT 1h: after a bar closes beyond a windowed prior swing level or a psychological round number, measure forward drift over the next K bars against a baseline.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: bar close beyond a prior swing support/resistance or round-number level. Invalidation: thesis is continuation-after-stop-run; invalidated if price reverts back inside the range within K bars (no vacuum), or if the breach occurs on declining stop-cluster density.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry at NEXT_BAR_CLOSE after breach; stop = back inside the broken level (swing point); target = next structure (R-multiple 1.0); expiry = K bars (book's time-based exits).
findings.quote: Research in the currencies markets indicated that once support (resistance) levels are breached, prices will go further down (up) for a while (Osler, 2000, 2001).
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch 7 High-Frequency Trading, pp.167-168 (stop hunting, Osler citation)
findings.notes: Cites Osler's empirical intraday FX work on post-breach continuation driven by stop clustering. Crypto perp: 24/7 stops always live, high leverage inflates stop clusters, and round-number/liquidation levels matter; 1h-bar testable. Overlaps the formalized failed_breakout / liquidity_sweep_reclaim families; the new element is the round-number location feature and the pre-breach manipulation narrative (HFT-only, not directly tradeable by us).
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Signed order flow predicts short-term price change
findings.setup_summary: Signed transaction volume (buys at ask minus sells at bid) accumulated over a look-back window predicts same-direction short-term price movement, because informed traders hit with market orders and market makers reprice. Falsifiable: regress next-interval return on trailing cumulative signed flow on BTCUSDT tape.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: cumulative/average signed order flow over the look-back is strongly positive (long) or negative (short). Invalidation: flow fails to predict (market makers already repriced), i.e., price does not follow flow direction within the horizon.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry next interval open/close; stop = opposite flow reversal; target = R-multiple; expiry = short fixed horizon.
findings.quote: Empirical research indicates that order flow information is a good predictor of price movements... order flow can predict short-term price movement in the same direction.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch 7 High-Frequency Trading, pp.167-168 (order flow, Lyons 2001)
findings.notes: V8's feature-group vocabulary already includes 'flow'; this supports adding signed-flow imbalance features to marketstate. Crypto perp tape is fully visible (buy/sell aggressor flags), so it is computable, but V8 consumes 1h bars and flow features need intra-bar aggregation; the book's use is tick/intraday scale, so 1h predictive power must be tested, not assumed.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Kelly optimal leverage as upper bound (half-Kelly sizing)
findings.setup_summary: Optimal leverage f = m/s^2 (Gaussian Kelly) maximizes compounded growth but estimation error in m and s means over-estimating leverage leads to ruin; therefore deploy at most half-Kelly and treat Kelly as an upper bound, never the operating leverage. Non-Gaussian reality is better handled by optimizing expected log-growth on Monte-Carlo returns matched to the first four moments (Pearson system) or directly on backtest returns.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Sizing rule only; falsifiable at portfolio level: an active risk rule that size exceeds 1/|worst observed bar return| must be rejected as ruin-in-sample.
findings.risk_geometry: Position size = leverage f on equity, capped at half-Kelly; hard ruin bound f < 1 / |max_negative_bar_return| (book's worked example: f=30.2 ruins on a -3.31% bar).
findings.quote: The consequence of using an overestimated mean or an underestimated variance is dire: Either case will lead to an overestimated optimal leverage, and if this overestimated leverage is high enough, it will eventually lead to ruin: equity going to zero.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Optimal Leverage, pp.171-177 (Kelly, Monte Carlo, historical growth)
findings.notes: Directly relevant to perp crypto where leverage is a free choice up to 100x+. Informative for V8's heat cap and position sizing: adds a Kelly-derived upper bound and the ruin bound f < 1/|worst return|. Note the constant-leverage corollary (see separate finding) is a contagion anti-pattern V8 should avoid.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Constant Proportion Portfolio Insurance (CPPI)
findings.setup_summary: To both cap maximum drawdown at -D and keep near-optimal growth: put only a fraction D of total equity in a trading subaccount and apply Kelly leverage f to it, keeping the rest in cash. Losses never draw cash from the subaccount (so size shrinks toward zero as drawdown grows), and at a new equity high-water mark the subaccount is reset to D of total equity. Doubling down on the drawdown-limit property: reducing leverage to cap drawdown is highly nonlinear (cutting f by ~7x was needed to halve simulated max DD from 0.999 to ~0.5).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Risk/lifecycle rule; falsifiable at portfolio level: with the scheme, realized account drawdown must never exceed -D on any backtested path, and order size must be monotonically decreasing in drawdown.
findings.risk_geometry: Size = f * D * equity; no stop loss needed; reset to D-of-equity at new high watermark; account wind-down when subaccount is exhausted.
findings.quote: We can simply set aside D of our initial total account equity for trading, and apply a leverage of f to this subaccount... We can then be assured that we won't... suffer a drawdown of more than -D in our total account... this scheme serves as a graceful, principled way to wind down a losing strategy.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Constant Proportion Portfolio Insurance, pp.179-182
findings.notes: A clean, deterministic drawdown-cap scheme that fits V8's gate architecture (no wall-clock, no learned component). Book notes CPPI is per-strategy (not for multistrategy accounts where winners subsidize losers) and cannot protect against overnight gaps/suspended markets - in 24/7 crypto the gap risk is lower but flash-crash wick risk remains (see flash_crash finding).
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Stop-loss placement is regime/strategy-class contingent
findings.setup_summary: For mean-reversion strategies a stop loss always lowers backtested Sharpe because of survivorship bias - the successful catalog excludes the mean-reverting series that regime-changed into trending - yet it prevents ruin when that regime change happens; so place the stop beyond the backtest maximum intraday drawdown so it never triggers in-sample but catches the black swan. For momentum strategies a continuously updated momentum signal is a de facto stop (loss means momentum reversed, so exit or reverse); stops are therefore a natural, low-cost component of momentum experts and remove the tail risk that mean-reversion experts carry.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Falsifiable: on an MR family, a stop placed inside the backtest max intraday drawdown must lower in-sample Sharpe; a stop placed beyond it must leave in-sample performance unchanged but truncate the worst OOS tail.
findings.risk_geometry: MR stops: beyond backtest max intraday drawdown (wide, rarely hit); momentum stops: signal reversal / time-based exits, no separate hard stop required.
findings.quote: It is more accurate to say that stop loss always lowers the performance of mean-reverting strategies when the prices remain mean reverting, but it certainly improves the performance of those strategies when the prices suffer a regime change and start to trend!... we should impose a stop loss that is greater than the backtest maximum intraday drawdown.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Stop Loss, pp.182-184
findings.notes: Distinguishes dead-thesis exits from stop exits in a way that maps onto V8's still_valid mechanism: for trend/momentum experts the still_valid signal is the stop (a la trend_pullback's uptrend-persists check); for future mean-reversion experts the stop must sit beyond the in-sample max drawdown. Also flags that a stop is only as good as continuous liquidity - relevant to crypto wick-throughs.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Leading risk indicators as regime filters (VIX/TED/order flow)
findings.setup_summary: Leading risk indicators (VIX, TED spread, HYG, MXN, ONN/OFF, and sudden large negative order flow on risky assets) can gate trading in the next period, but they are strategy-specific: VIX>35 was good for the buy-on-gap stock strategy (Sharpe 1.5->1.4, return 8.7%->17.2%) yet catastrophic for the FSTX opening-gap strategy (return 13%->2.6%, Sharpe 1.4->0.16). The filter must therefore be validated per strategy, and backtesting rare crises invites data-snooping.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Falsifiable per strategy: the indicator's high state must shift the conditional forward return distribution of that strategy (measured OOS). Invalidation: no shift, or the shift flips sign OOS.
findings.risk_geometry: Regime gate only: skip entries (or reduce size) while the indicator is in its risky state; no position-level geometry.
findings.quote: If the preceding day's VIX is over 35, then the day's annualized average return drops to 2.6 percent and the Sharpe ratio to 0.16. Clearly, VIX tells us to avoid trading on the following day.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Risk Indicators, pp.184-186
findings.notes: For perp crypto the VIX/TED analogs are less clean; candidate leading indicators are funding-rate extremes, basis, and perp aggregate open-interest/leverage - these are observable 24/7 (no VIX open-to-close regime). Lesson for V8: a regime filter is strategy-specific, so it belongs per expert (registry-gated), and backtests over rare crises are data-snoop-prone.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Kelly capital allocation under a binding leverage cap concentrates
findings.setup_summary: With multiple strategies and a broker/account gross-leverage cap Fmax much smaller than the sum of individual Kelly leverages, proportionally scaling all positions down (the naive fix) is suboptimal; the worked two-strategy example shows concentrating all buying power into the strategy with the highest independent growth rate (F2=Fmax) beats the proportional scaling (growth 0.96 vs 0.82). Applicable whenever a portfolio-level leverage constraint binds.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Portfolio-level: given two uncorrelated strategies and a binding gross leverage cap, concentrating in the highest-growth one yields higher compounded growth than proportional scaling (book's Example 8.2).
findings.risk_geometry: No position geometry; allocation rule over strategies, relevant only when a portfolio leverage/heat constraint binds.
findings.quote: The upshot of that example is that when Fmax is much smaller than sum|Fi|, it is often optimal (with respect to maximizing the growth rate) to just invest most or all our buying power into the portfolio or strategy with the highest mean excess return.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Example 8.2, pp.173-175
findings.notes: V8 has no ranker/router (absent by default, gated), so this is a recorded methodology lesson for any future allocation layer rather than an implementable component; it also cautions against a naive 'scale everything down' heat-cap implementation once multiple experts are active.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Stop-loss protection is contingent on continuous liquidity
findings.setup_summary: A stop loss only guarantees a maximum loss if a market is open with liquidity present: in the May 6 2010 flash crash, market makers withdrew to stub quotes ($0.01) and a stop on Accenture executed at $0.01. Stops also cannot protect across overnight gaps or suspended markets. Implication: execution models and risk gates must assume stop fills degrade in liquidity-withdrawal states rather than always filling near the stop price.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Falsifiable in simulation: modeled stop slippage under a low-liquidity/high-volatility state must be materially worse than the normal-state fill price; a simulator that always fills stops at their limit price overstates protection.
findings.risk_geometry: Stop fills: gap-through/slippage modeling in stressed states; no protection assumed across market suspension.
findings.quote: In some extreme circumstances, stop loss is useless even if the market is open but when all liquidity providers decide to withdraw their liquidity simultaneously. This happened during the flash crash of May 6, 2010... an unfortunate sell stop order on Accenture... was executed at $0.01 per share that day.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Stop Loss, p.183 (flash crash, Arnuk & Saluzzi 2012)
findings.notes: Crypto perp has no traditional gaps (24/7) so stop-loss gap risk is reduced, but liquidity can still vanish in deleveraging cascades and liquidation-engine wicks can trade through stop levels by large multiples; V8's canonical simulator (STOP_FIRST, fill-at-close, gap semantics) should model stop slippage under stress states rather than assuming limit fills.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Constant-leverage rebalancing 'selling into losses' is a contagion amplifier
findings.setup_summary: Optimal-leverage schemes require keeping leverage constant: after a loss you must sell into the loss and after a gain buy more. When many funds hold similar positions and all follow constant-leverage risk management, one fund's forced liquidation forces others to liquidate - cited as a cause of the August 2007 quant meltdown (Khandani & Lo 2007). Sizing/rebalancing rules that mechanically de-leverage into drawdowns shared across the market amplify the drawdown they are meant to cap.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Macro-level, not directly testable on one expert; the falsifiable version is that forced leverage-rebalance selling co-moves with other funds' liquidations during stress.
findings.risk_geometry: None at position level; design caution for the sizing/heat-cap rule.
findings.quote: This is because often many funds are holding similar positions in their portfolios. If one fund suffers losses... it is prone to liquidate positions across all its portfolios due to the constant leverage requirement, causing losses for all other funds that hold those positions... a vicious cycle.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch 8 Risk Management - Example 8.1: The Implications of the Constant Leverage Requirement, pp.170-171
findings.notes: Directly relevant to crypto liquidation cascades (funding + leverage concentration). Design inference for V8: do not implement forced constant-leverage rebalancing that sells into losses; a heat cap or CPPI-style monotonically-shrinking size is safer than re-leveraging on the way down.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Hypothesis-first, falsifiable, OOS-tested strategy research
findings.setup_summary: Strategy development is a scientific loop: form a hypothesis about a specific market inefficiency, express it as a simple quantitative model, test against new unseen data, and when it underperforms seek a fundamental cause (e.g., the GLD/GDX pair stopped cointegrating until crude-oil was added) rather than piling on arbitrary rules. Simple linear models exploit an understood inefficiency; regime shifts and non-stationarity are why live-vs-backtest divergence happens, and the manager's role is high-level validity judgment while algorithms beat experts at rule execution (Kahneman).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Process standard, not a strategy: a research action is invalid if it adds rules/indicators without a stated falsifiable mechanism and an OOS test.
findings.risk_geometry: None.
findings.quote: In science, we form a hypothesis, express it as a quantitative model, and then test it against new, unseen data to see if the model is predictive... Instead of blindly adding more rules, more indicators... we should look for a fundamental reason and then quantitatively test whether this fundamental reason is valid.
findings.chapter_anchor: Conclusion, pp.187-189
findings.notes: This is the book's core epistemology and matches V8's falsification mandate (evidence labels, frozen OOS, challenger-vs-registry evolution). Reinforces V8 rules: mechanism-first family design, no arbitrary rule accretion, registry-gated evolution, and evidence-bound claims.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

book_title: Algorithmic Trading: Winning Strategies and Their Rationale (E. Chan, 2013) - Part 2

findings.strategy_name: Crisis hunting: positive-skew harvesting of rare events
findings.mechanism: Rare events are systematically underpriced (the rarer, the more undervalued), so engineer a payoff profile that loses small and frequent and pays large and rare
findings.setup_summary: Construct every expert's risk_geometry with positive skew: bounded small frequent losses (tight stop, small R) against rare large gains (wide target, large R), so expectation is positive even at a win rate below 50%. On BTCUSDT 1h this is the payoff profile of tight-stop trend/crisis-hunting variants that let tails pay. The book also states the binding companion rule (Nero): never expose to a loss exceeding a fixed cap 'regardless of the probability of such an event' — i.e., no unbounded-loss (short-convexity) position is ever admissible.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any setup whose payoff is constructed asymmetric-positive. Invalid: expectation goes negative under honest fat-tail calibration (Monte Carlo with realistic kurtosis), or realized drawdown breaches the designed bounded cap.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: bar close or limit at tail levels; stop: small R (tight ATR multiple); target: large R-multiple, left open so rare moves pay; expiry: long/open-ended. Book states only the payoff profile (small frequent losses, rare large gains); R-multiples are V8's expression.
findings.quote: I try to make money infrequently, as infrequently as possible, simply because I believe that rare events are not fairly valued, and that the rarer the event, the more undervalued it will be in price.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 6, Rare Events (p. 89); Nero's cap in Ch. 1 (p. 15)
findings.notes: Book-side quantitative case: 999/1000 chance of +$1 vs 1/1000 chance of -$10,000 is a -$9 expectation. 'Premium sellers eat like chickens and go to the bathroom like elephants' — most option sellers blow up. For perps (no native options), the positive-skew posture is expressed via asymmetric R-multiples and hard max-loss caps; high leverage makes the bounded-loss rule mandatory.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Predetermined falsification stop (black-swan protection)
findings.mechanism: Define in advance which price event falsifies the thesis, and exit mechanically on it; the stop is a predetermined exit point that protects against the rare event
findings.setup_summary: Before entry, specify the observable event that proves the conjecture wrong; pre-place an exit at that level and honor it mechanically when price reaches it or the thesis is invalidated. It is distinct from profit-taking and is the accepted protection of the surviving traders described in the book ('All the surviving traders I know seem to have done the same').
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: entry taken with a pre-specified falsification level. Invalid: price trades through the stop and the exit is deferred; or the thesis was entered with no falsification level defined at all.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: any; stop: predetermined exit point ('a stop loss, a predetermined exit point'); target/expiry not specified; exit is thesis-falsification-based and separate from the profit target.
findings.quote: This is called a stop loss, a predetermined exit point, a protection from the black swan. I find it rarely practiced.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 7, Pascal's Wager (p. 110)
findings.notes: Directly reinforces V8's distinction between the risk_geometry stop and the dead-thesis (still_valid) exit, and the Popperian requirement that a hypothesis state its own refutation conditions. The anti-pattern is Carlos's 'stop losses are for schmucks' denial. Crypto 24/7 + high leverage: no exchange-gap excuse, forced liquidation is the stop you didn't set.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Unplanned averaging down (blowup trait)
findings.mechanism: Adding to a losing position on dips without a pre-planned conditional rule and without a stop converts a temporary dip into ruin when the dip does not reverse
findings.setup_summary: Anti-pattern: buy every 'line in the sand' as price falls, relying on a 'value'/narrative thesis while price keeps declining, with no predetermined stop and no plan for the event of continued decline. Carlos added Russian bonds at $52, $43, $30s, $20s — then sub-$10 — converting cumulative +$80M into a single -$300M quarter. The trait that made dip-buyers the 1992-1998 winners was the same trait that killed them in 1998.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any add-to-loser must be a pre-registered conditional rule with its own risk budget. Invalid: discretionary averaging-down with no plan; price breaks the registered add-condition or the pre-registered stop.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: bar close or limit after dips; stop: none (that is the failure mode); target: none; expiry: none — the anti-pattern is the absence of any pre-planned geometry.
findings.quote: Both bought more bonds after the market declined sharply, but not in response to a predetermined plan.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5, A Review of Market Fools of Randomness Constants (p. 79-80)
findings.notes: Correlates with V8 position_scaling concept but inverts it: scaling into losers is admissible only as a registered conditional rule (one multiplicity unit with its own geometry), never as discretionary 'value' buying. On perps, averaging down without a stop compounds toward liquidation.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Data snooping / backtest overfitting as survivorship in rule space
findings.mechanism: Trying many parameterizations on history guarantees a spurious past winner; a random series always presents some detectable pattern, so rules that survive are survivors, not genuine edge
findings.setup_summary: Methodology: iterating a rule's parameters until it 'works' on past data ('buy NASDAQ if close more than 1.83% above prior-week average', then 1.2%, then more complex rules) is the same as looking for the survivor within the set of rules. The book cites Sullivan, Timmerman and White: if enough parameterizations are tried over time, some will look superior by pure luck even with no true predictive power. V8 consequence: parameter variants are one multiplicity unit and must be judged on frozen OOS not used in fitting, with the full variant count disclosed.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any rule judged on past data. Invalid: rule fails to hold on frozen OOS; performance collapses when the snooping-adjusted significance (cohort of variants tried) is computed.
findings.risk_geometry: n/a — methodology lesson, no trade geometry.
findings.quote: The more I try, the more I am likely, by mere luck, to find a rule that worked on past data. A random series will always present some detectable pattern.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 9, The Backtester (p. 134-135)
findings.notes: Also covers the birthday-paradox / cancer-cluster / spurious-correlation argument ('I am convinced that there exists a tradable security... 100% correlated with the changes in temperature in Oulan Bator'). Directly supports V8's multiplicity-unit rule and the challenger + frozen-OOS + registry protocol (rule 15/14).
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Expectation (probability x payoff), not hit rate, decides the trade
findings.mechanism: The check is expectation = probability x payoff; frequency/probability alone is irrelevant without the magnitude of the outcome
findings.setup_summary: Methodology: evaluate any strategy by expectation over its outcome distribution, never by win rate or directional accuracy. The book's worked example: 70% chance of +1% and 30% chance of -10% is net -2.3 — 'bullish' yet correctly shorted. A 90%-losing option position can still be the better side if the winning 10% pays 50x.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any expert evaluation. Invalid: strategy shows positive hit-rate but negative expectation, or expectation turns negative on honest out-of-sample distribution estimation.
findings.risk_geometry: n/a — evaluation methodology.
findings.quote: it is not how likely an event is to happen that matters, it is how much is made when it happens that should be the consideration.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 6, Bull and Bear Zoology (p. 88)
findings.notes: 'Bullish or bearish are terms used by people who do not engage in practicing uncertainty.' For V8: expert scoring must be expectation-based over the simulated outcome distribution (simulator STOP_FIRST, cost model), not accuracy-based; mirrors the 'you are paid in dollars, not probabilities' point.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Observation-frequency effect: at short scales you see variance, not returns
findings.mechanism: The noise:signal ratio explodes as the observation scale shrinks (1796:1 at one second for a 15%/10% process), so high-frequency monitoring misreads variance as signal
findings.setup_summary: Methodology: a 15% return / 10% volatility process has a 93% probability of profit over a year but only 50.02% over a second; over one hour there are ~30 parts noise per part performance, over one second ~1796. Judge strategies on longer-window aggregates and never treat short-window P&L as evidence; the same strategy evaluated monthly vs daily is the same strategy with different emotional load.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any evaluation of an expert. Invalid: conclusions flip when the same strategy is evaluated on a longer observation scale; short-window P&L treated as signal.
findings.risk_geometry: n/a — evaluation methodology; book notes the negative pang is up to 2.5x the positive one, so emotional reaction to short-window noise is systematically costly.
findings.quote: Over a short time increment, one observes the variability of the portfolio, not the returns.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 3, Philostratus in Monte Carlo (p. 58), Table 3.1
findings.notes: Crypto is 24/7, so the temptation to observe continuously is maximal; the lesson supports V8's bar-level determinism (no wall clock in replay), its event/available/ingested clock discipline, and longer-window registry evaluation instead of reacting to short-window equity moves.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Leveraged carry blowup: correlation breakdown plus mis-estimated tail
findings.mechanism: A small positive-carry spread multiplied by leverage and 'protected' by hedges blows up when hedges break down together and the tail probability was mis-estimated from short history (the 'ten sigma' error)
findings.setup_summary: John's trade: borrow at ~5.5%, buy ~10% 'cheap' bonds (net 4.5% carry), hedge interest-rate exposure with government-bond futures, levered to ~$50M book on ~$14M equity. The 1998 event: everything went against him at once, hedges failed together, and the model put the event at 'ten sigma' (1 in 10^24 years). The book's lesson: model-derived probabilities from recent history understate rare-event frequency by orders of magnitude, and correlation breakdown under stress invalidates the hedge.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: leveraged carry with hedges. Invalid: hedges exhibit correlation breakdown under stress (correlations go to 1), carry flips, or realized tail frequency exceeds the model estimate.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: long carry asset / short hedge (futures); leverage ~3.6x implied; stop: none effective; target: carry yield plus convergence; expiry: ongoing; failure mode: leveraged unwind. Note: 'a small loss would be compounded and would wipe him out'.
findings.quote: The effect of the leverage is that a small loss would be compounded and would wipe him out.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5, The Quant Who Knew Computers and Equations (p. 76-77)
findings.notes: Crypto analog is direct: funding carry and basis trades are native to perps, leverage is extreme, and deleveraging cascades/flash crashes are documented. Maps to correlated_exposure_cap and max_drawdown_cap rules, plus a simulator requirement to model stress correlation breakdown rather than permanent hedge offset. The 'ten sigma' point also feeds the stationarity finding (NEW_crowded_pattern_stationarity).
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Cross-sectional problem: recent winners are best-fit to the latest cycle
findings.mechanism: At any point the most profitable operators are those best fit to the most recent cycle, not the most skilled; ergodicity reverts them over a longer sample path
findings.setup_summary: Methodology: dip-buying was the trait most desirable from 1992 to summer 1998 in emerging/high-yield markets; the dip-buyers dominated and displaced arguably better traders, then blew up together in 1998 when the regime flipped. 'The richest traders are often the worst traders' at any cross-section. For V8: an expert's recent top performance is regime-conditional, so registry promotion must be evidence-bound across regime samples, not extrapolated from the latest winners.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any registry promotion decision. Invalid: recent top performance reverses across regime samples; no regime-conditional evaluation was run.
findings.risk_geometry: n/a — evaluation/registry methodology.
findings.quote: at a given time in the market, the most profitable traders are likely to be those that are best fit to the latest cycle.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5, Carlos the Emerging Markets Wizard (p. 74)
findings.notes: Supports a regime_filter methodology component: crypto alternates sharply between trending and ranging regimes; a strategy's pedigree (e.g., 'this worked in the last 2 years') must be discounted for regime fit. Ties to ergodicity: 'The lucky fool... over the longer run he would slowly converge to the state of a less-lucky idiot.'
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Track-record validity depends on cohort size, not individual skill
findings.mechanism: Observed track records are draws from a cohort; the expected maximum of records depends more on cohort size and volatility than on individual odds, so even incompetent populations produce great-looking records
findings.setup_summary: Methodology: in a fair 50/50 game, 10,000 managers yield ~313 with five consecutive winning years by pure chance; even a cohort of expected losers (45/55) yields ~184 five-year survivors, and 'volatility actually helps bad investment decisions.' The validity of any track record requires knowing the size of the cohort it was drawn from — 10 managers is meaningful, 10,000 is noise. V8 consequence: report the multiplicity of variants/experts screened when evaluating any record, and treat unsolicited/adverse-selected records as near-meaningless.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: track-record-based acceptance of any strategy. Invalid: after cohort-size adjustment the record is consistent with pure chance; no replication outside the original cohort.
findings.risk_geometry: n/a — evaluation methodology.
findings.quote: the expectation of the maximum of track records... depends more on the size of the initial sample, than on the individual odds per manager.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 9, Nobody Has To Be Competent (p. 129-130)
findings.notes: Also grounds the adverse-selection rule: 'the chance of the soliciting party being a spurious survivor is closer to 100%' when the record comes to you. Directly supports V8's registry stages (SCREENING/REPLICATION/SHADOW) and the frozen-OOS evidence gate.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Consensus narrative overriding price (firehouse effect)
findings.mechanism: A narrative shared and reinforced among peers ('it's only a liquidation', 'sell-off is overdone', 'too big to fail') anchors the thesis and overrides price evidence; the price is the un-fooled referee
findings.setup_summary: Anti-pattern: Carlos's hour-long daily calls with market economists all saying 'this sell-off is overdone' and 'Russia will not go under', plus self-justification via 'other banks have bigger losses' (the firehouse effect: people who talk to each other too long come to agree on things an outside observer finds ludicrous). The thesis was never anchored to price; the bonds fell from $52 to below $10. Lesson: keep thesis invalidation strictly price-based; narrative/story inputs cannot override price evidence, and a statement 'that other traders also got into trouble' is self-incriminating.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: thesis supported only by narrative. Invalid: price action violates the narrative-anchored level; 'overdone' stories coincide with continued price decline.
findings.risk_geometry: n/a — behavioral/methodology lesson.
findings.quote: the price of the bonds was not fooled. It knew more than the economists, more than the Carloses of the emerging market departments.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5, Lines in the Sand / Averaging Down (p. 72-73)
findings.notes: Crypto has extremely strong liquidation/panic narratives (funding flushes, forced-seller stories, 'this time is different'). For V8, the lesson is methodological: never let a news/narrative feature override price-based feature evidence; the mechanical, price-only design already encodes this. The 'these times are different' historical-denial pattern (Ch. 3, The Stove Is Hot) is the same family.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Lucas critique / non-stationarity: detectable patterns get arbitraged away
findings.mechanism: The data-generating process is non-stationary (a 'mischievous child' replaces the balls), and any pattern detectable to everyone is ironed out as soon as it is acted upon
findings.setup_summary: Methodology: the mischievous-child/urn argument shows inference from a single past time series is shaky when the process changes; the Lucas critique shows any publicly detectable pattern (e.g., Monday effect) is arbitraged away by anticipatory buying, so 'there is no point searching for patterns that are available to everyone with a brokerage account.' For V8: expect decay in any simple, widely-known pattern; test stationarity explicitly and re-validate experts on frozen OOS; treat 'it has never happened before' as no evidence at all (the market-never-drops-20%-in-a-quarter example is unfalsifiable by confirmation).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: pattern-based expert. Invalid: pattern returns decay as participation/volume on it grows; OOS performance erodes while in-sample held.
findings.risk_geometry: n/a — methodology lesson.
findings.quote: If rational traders detect a pattern of stocks rising on Mondays, then, immediately such a pattern becomes detectable, it would be ironed out by people buying on Friday in anticipation of such an effect.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 6, A Mischievous Child Replaces the Black Balls (p. 97-98)
findings.notes: Crypto TA and funding/fee patterns are widely shared and crowd quickly. Pairs with the black-swan asymmetry: 'our knowledge about the absence of red balls will increase very slowly... our knowledge of the presence of red balls will dramatically improve once one of them is found' — supports falsification (data disproves, never proves), which is V8's constitution (rule 12 evidence-bound, rule 15 frozen OOS).
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Valuation overshoot reversion (Shiller)
findings.mechanism: Prices overreact to fundamentals, running too high on good news and too low on bad, then revert toward the fundamental proxy
findings.setup_summary: Shiller's 1981 finding (cited in the book): if a price is the estimated value of discounted cash flows, then market prices are far too volatile relative to the fundamentals they reflect — visibly overshooting in both directions, which contradicts rational-expectation efficiency. Tradeable family for crypto perps: build a value proxy (funding/basis, realized-vol-based fair range, or carry) and fade price when it deviates by a large multiple of the proxy, expecting reversion.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: extreme price-vs-proxy deviation. Invalid: proxy keeps expanding (funding/basis stays extreme) with no reversion within the expiry horizon; regime change breaks the proxy.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: bar close or limit at the extreme; stop: beyond the valuation proxy by a multiple; target: reversion to proxy mean; expiry: bounded (weeks-to-months scale per the book's 'market is too volatile relative to fundamentals' claim).
findings.quote: Prices swing more than the fundamentals they are supposed to reflect, they visibly overreact by being too high at times (when their price overshoots the good news or when they go up without any marked reason) or too low at others.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 3, Shiller Redux (p. 53-54)
findings.notes: The book states the inefficiency and overreaction but not a tradable setup, so this is a backlog family candidate gated on a defensible perp value proxy (no clean dividends/cash flows for BTC). The book also notes the peso-problem corollary: 'currencies that exhibit the largest historical stability are the most prone to crashes' — calm-waters regimes precede violent breaks, relevant to volatility-compression fade setups.
findings.book: Fooled by Randomness - The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets 2005

findings.strategy_name: Z-score / Bollinger band mean reversion on a stationary series (entry/exit z-score levels)
findings.mechanism: an OU-style pull toward a moving mean is exploitable only within a band; enter on deviation, exit on reversion to the mean
findings.setup_summary: On a stationary or cointegrated price/spread series with a short half-life, enter long when z-score = (price - movingAvg)/(movingStd) crosses below -entryZscore, exit when it reverts to -exitZscore (e.g., 0); short is the mirror. One unit at a time (all-in). Author backtest on the GLD-USO spread: APR 17.8%, Sharpe 0.96 (no transaction costs; prototype). Lookback can be set to the half-life instead of optimized.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: z-score beyond entryZscore band on a series that passed stationarity/half-life gating. Invalidation: the series stops reverting - z-score fails to reach exitZscore within a horizon, or half-life lengthens / cointegration breaks (as GLD-GDX did after the July 2008 oil spike).
findings.risk_geometry: Entry NEXT_BAR_CLOSE on the spread/portfolio; target = exitZscore (0 = current mean); stop = none by design (stops contradict mean reversion, see risk-rule finding); expiry = small multiple of half-life lookback.
findings.quote: we can enter into a position only when the price deviates by more than entryZscore standard deviations from the mean... We can exit when the price mean-reverts to exitZscore standard deviations from the mean
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 3, 'Bollinger Bands' / Example 3.2 (see also Chapter 2 linear strategy)
findings.notes: Directly testable on BTCUSDT 1h price or on a funding/basis spread series; requires the stationarity/half-life gate (next finding) before admission. entryZscore/exitZscore/lookback become family variants, one multiplicity unit.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Stationarity and half-life gating before any mean-reversion trading
findings.mechanism: only series whose next move depends on current level (ADF lambda<0) or whose variance diffuses sublinearly (Hurst<0.5, VR test) can profit from mean reversion; half-life sets the natural time scale
findings.setup_summary: Before trading a series mean-reverting, run the ADF test (lambda/SE, 90%+ level), Hurst exponent (H<0.5), and Variance Ratio test; then regress deltaY on lag(Y) to get lambda and half-life = -log(2)/lambda. Only trade series that are stationary (or cointegrating, via CADF or Johansen eigenvector) with half-life short enough for the trading horizon. Set lookback and holding period to a small multiple of the half-life instead of brute-force optimization. A positive or near-zero lambda means do not trade it mean-reverting.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Half-life too long for the horizon, or lambda positive, rejects the mean-reversion model for that series; revalidate when the cointegration relationship breaks (e.g., GLD-GDX).
findings.risk_geometry: No trade geometry; it is a parameter-selection method (lookback = c x half-life).
findings.quote: this lambda also determines a natural time scale for many parameters in our strategy... Often, setting the look-back to equal a small multiple of the half-life is close to optimal
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 2, 'Half-Life of Mean Reversion' (ADF, Hurst/Variance Ratio, CADF, Johansen)
findings.notes: V8 gating rule: a mean-reversion family Expert should only be admitted when a point-in-time stationarity/half-life gate passes on the traded series or spread; this is a methodology/lifecycle input, not a strategy. Important because most price series (incl. BTC) are geometric random walks and will fail the gate.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: All-in beats scaling-in in-sample (Schoenberg-Corwin); scaling-in only defensible OOS
findings.mechanism: expected-profit comparison over two possible paths shows averaging-in is never the most profitable entry policy for any fixed transition probability; only time-varying volatility/probability justifies it
findings.setup_summary: For a mean-reversion target F with intermediate level L1 and deeper level L2 (reached with probability p), expected profits show: all-in at L1 dominates if p < p_hat = (F-L1)/(F-L2), all-in at L2 dominates if p > p_hat, and averaging-in (1 unit at L1 + 1 at L2) is never best. Because volatility - hence p - is not constant, scaling-in can still outperform out-of-sample, but it is never optimal in-sample and requires unbounded capital in the linear formulation.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Scaling-in justified only under time-varying volatility/probabilities; otherwise single all-in level dominates.
findings.risk_geometry: Single all-in entry level for mean-reversion entries; avoids the unlimited-capital requirement of linear z-score scaling.
findings.quote: entering or exiting at two or more Bollinger bands is never optimal; that is, you can always find a single entry/exit level that will generate a higher average return in a backtest
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 3, 'Does Scaling-in Work?' (Schoenberg and Corwin, 2010)
findings.notes: V8 rule of thumb: mean-reversion experts enter all-in at one z-score level, no pyramiding; position_scaling variants should be added only if a frozen-OOS comparison beats the all-in baseline.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Time-series momentum driven by persistence of the roll-return (carry) sign
findings.mechanism: when carry (roll yield) dominates and keeps its sign, total returns acquire serial correlation; in crypto perps the funding rate is the carry
findings.setup_summary: Futures time-series momentum (buy a future with a positive 12-month return, hold ~1 month; Moskowitz-Yao-Pedersen) is largely explained by the persistence of the sign of roll returns rather than spot moves. Cleaner signal: go long when the lagged annualized roll return exceeds a threshold (3% for TU), short when below -threshold, flat otherwise - TU APR 2.5%, Sharpe 2.1, max DD 1.1%. Crypto analog: perp funding rate; persistent positive funding (perps above spot) predicts continued perp outperformance.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Carry sign flips or carry magnitude collapses; regime shifts such as post-crisis momentum crashes.
findings.risk_geometry: Time-based exit: fixed holding period (~25 bars); a stop-loss is consistent with this family (unlike mean reversion).
findings.quote: Typically, the sign of roll returns does not vary very often... So if we hold a future over a long period of time, and if the average roll returns dominate the average total returns, we will find serial correlation of total returns.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 6, 'Time Series Strategies' + Chapter 5, 'Roll Returns, Backwardation, and Contango' (Example 6.1, Table 6.2)
findings.notes: Requires a funding-history feature (funding rate per bar) not yet in the V8 feature-group vocabulary (flow/cross_market extension). Directly falsifiable on BTCUSDT funding data.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Calendar-spread / term-structure mean reversion on roll return gamma, and spot-vs-future roll extraction
findings.mechanism: the log calendar spread equals gamma*(T1-T2); its signal depends only on the mean-reverting roll return gamma, not on the spot, so carry reversion is tradeable separately from price
findings.setup_summary: Long-far/short-near calendar spread: log value = gamma*(T1-T2), so the spread signal is driven entirely by gamma (estimated by regressing log futures prices on time-to-maturity). CL 12-month calendar spread: ADF stationary at 99%, half-life 36 days, linear mean-reversion APR 8.3%, Sharpe 1.3. Equivalent spot-extraction trade: buy the underlying asset (or a producer ETF) and short the future under contango, reverse in backwardation (GLD vs GC: 1.9% annualized, max DD 0.8%; XLE-USO: APR 16%). Crypto analog: perp (spot-anchored) vs quarterly futures basis and persistent funding.
findings.trigger_invalidation: gamma stops mean-reverting (persistently one-sided term structure); the underlying is not a tradeable asset (VX case: model 5.7 breaks).
findings.risk_geometry: Roll to next contract pair 10 days before near expiry; ~3-month holding; signal reversal when z-score of gamma crosses zero.
findings.quote: the calendar spread trading signal does not depend at all on the spot price, only on the roll return!
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 5, 'Trading Futures Calendar Spread' (Example 5.4) + Chapter 6, 'Extracting Roll Returns through Future versus ETF Arbitrage'
findings.notes: DATA_BLOCKED for V8: needs a derivatives tape (quarterly futures term structure and/or funding history) before coding, same gating as breakout_retest. In crypto the perp-vs-spot carry is realized via funding, and the perp-vs-quarterly basis is a live instrument on major venues.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Mean reversion of volatility and volatility-index anti-correlation (VX-ES stationary portfolio)
findings.mechanism: volatility is stationary and anti-correlated with the underlying index, so a constant-hedge-ratio long-vol/long-index portfolio is stationary and band-tradeable
findings.setup_summary: The VIX index is stationary by ADF at 99%, but VX front futures are in persistent contango (average annualized roll return about -50%) so VX price itself does not mean-revert; the VX back/front ratio does (ADF stationary at 99%, linear MR APR 17.7%, Sharpe 1.5). Volatility is strongly anti-correlated with the equity index (VX-ES daily-return correlation about -75%): a stationary portfolio long 0.3906 VX + long 1 ES (prices scaled by contract multipliers), traded with a Bollinger band on the regression residuals, gives APR 12.3%, Sharpe 1.4 on the test set.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Volatility regime change (author documents two regimes 2004-2008 vs 2008-2012: lower level, wider range); correlation breaks; mixing regimes invalidates the regression/hedge ratio.
findings.risk_geometry: Bollinger entry at +-1 std of stationary-portfolio residuals; hedge ratio fixed from a 500-day training set, then traded out-of-sample.
findings.quote: volatility is anti-correlated with the stock equity market index: When the market goes down, volatility shoots up, and to a lesser extent, vice versa
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 5, 'Volatility Futures versus Equity Index Futures' (Figure 5.10-5.12)
findings.notes: V8 has no vol instrument; implement as a realized-volatility feature (from OHLC) and a vol-mean-reversion regime/filter gate rather than a traded expert. The regime-split warning (do not regress across regimes) is directly applicable to V8 gating.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Post-event announcement drift: momentum from slow information diffusion
findings.mechanism: price adjustments to new information complete gradually, so the market's own initial reaction direction persists into the session
findings.setup_summary: After an earnings announcement made between prior close and today's open, buy at the open if the close-to-open return >= 0.5*std (90-day close-to-open std) and short if <= -0.5*std, liquidate at the same day's close. SPX universe: APR 6.7%, Sharpe 1.5 (Jan 2011-Apr 2012); overnight returns are on average negative. The trader does not interpret the news - the market's reaction is the signal. Duration of the drift has compressed from days (known since 1968) to intraday as awareness grew; other events (guidance, M&A, index composition changes) show the same pattern.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Drift shortens below the bar horizon; announcement elicits no surprise (small reaction); macro news (FOMC, CPI) shows no significant drift in EURUSD.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry at session open, exit at same-session close; intraday, no overnight carry; ~30 positions max daily.
findings.quote: this move will persist for some time after the announcement, and in the same direction, allowing momentum traders to benefit
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 7, 'Post-Earnings Announcement Drift' (Example 7.2) and 'Drift Due to Other Events'
findings.notes: DATA_BLOCKED for V8: needs an event calendar/news feed for crypto (listings, regulatory, halvings, macro). The transferable principles: use the market's reaction, not your interpretation, and expect drift duration to decay as crowding increases.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Forced asset sales/purchases and constant-leverage rebalancing generate momentum
findings.mechanism: mechanical flows (redemptions, inflows, constant-leverage rebalancing) buy and sell regardless of price, pushing prices in the flow direction and creating serial momentum that later reverts
findings.setup_summary: Mutual funds facing >5% redemptions sell existing holdings, depressing prices and contagiously hurting other funds holding the same names; inflows cause the mirror (Coval-Stafford PRESSURE factor; market-neutral decile portfolio about 17% annualized, front-running predicted flows another 17%, post-pressure reversion 7%). Leveraged ETFs rebalancing to constant leverage near the close force buying after up days and selling after down days: buy DRN if the return to 15 minutes before close exceeds 2%, sell if below -2%, exit at close - APR 15%, Sharpe 1.8; a 1% SPX move needs ~17% of market-on-close volume traded by these funds. Crypto analog: liquidation cascades and funding-driven forced flows.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Flow factor neutralized by offsetting investor flows; regime where flow-driven momentum reverses (August 2007 quant meltdown).
findings.risk_geometry: PRESSURE factor: quarterly rebalance; leveraged-ETF trade: intraday entry/exit at close; time-based exits.
findings.quote: Stocks disproportionately held by poorly performing mutual funds facing redemptions therefore experience negative returns. Furthermore, this asset 'fire sale'... is contagious.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 6, 'Mutual Funds Asset Fire Sale and Forced Purchases' + Chapter 7, 'Leveraged ETF Strategy'
findings.notes: Closest crypto analog in the starter vocabulary is deleveraging_cascade (liquidation flows); would require a liquidation/funding flow feature group. The two-stage behavior (momentum during forced flow, reversion after) is the falsifiable core.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Momentum crashes and regime alternation between momentum and mean reversion
findings.mechanism: after a crisis, the rebound of crowded short positions and forced flows replaces momentum with strong mean reversion for years
findings.setup_summary: Time-series and cross-sectional momentum strategies perform miserably for years after financial crises (Daniel-Moskowitz): the S&P DTI index was down -25.9% since Dec 2008; cross-sectional stock momentum was APR -30% in 2008-2009; after 1929 a representative momentum strategy took over 30 years to regain its high-water mark. Mean reversion is replaced by / replaces momentum regime-wise. Momentum thrives on kurtosis/black-swan events and is easy to risk-manage (limited downside); mean reversion has capped upside and can gap to catastrophic loss at max leverage.
findings.trigger_invalidation: None ex-ante - this is a regime gate, not a tradable trigger; cannot be known in advance.
findings.risk_geometry: Regime filter on strategy admission and leverage rather than trade geometry; frozen-OOS evidence must span crisis periods.
findings.quote: research by Daniel and Moskowitz on 'momentum crashes' indicates that momentum strategies for futures or stocks tend to perform miserably for several years after a financial crisis
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 6, 'Pros and Cons of Momentum Strategies' (see also Chapter 1 regime-shift section)
findings.notes: V8 implication: any momentum/carry expert needs a crisis/post-crisis regime gate, and OOS evidence is not credible unless it includes at least one crisis episode. Crypto analogues include the 2021-05 and 2022 deleveraging crashes.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Stop-losses are structurally inconsistent with mean-reversion entries; time-based exits fit momentum
findings.mechanism: a stop below a mean-reversion entry sits exactly where the reversion thesis strengthens, so stops contradict the entry logic; momentum entries have natural stop semantics (signal reversal)
findings.setup_summary: Momentum strategies support both time-based and stop-loss exits (a reversed signal acts as a natural stop); downside is bounded, upside unlimited. Mean-reversion strategies cannot use stops without contradicting their entry signal - their upside is capped at the mean while downside is unbounded, so risk must be managed via position sizing, leverage, and the natural profit cap, not stops. Stop losses are also useless in markets that close (gap risk); 24/7 markets avoid the gap problem but not the logic contradiction.
findings.trigger_invalidation: N/A - design rule.
findings.risk_geometry: For mean-reversion experts: no ATR stop; use expiry/time-out and dead-thesis exit plus sized exposure. For momentum experts: stop and time exits both valid.
findings.quote: stop losses are not consistent with mean-reverting strategies, because they contradict mean reversion strategies' entry signals
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 6, 'Pros and Cons of Momentum Strategies' (extended in Chapter 8, in Part 2)
findings.notes: Direct input to V8 RiskGate: a hard atr_stop on a mean-reversion family is structurally wrong. V8's still_valid/dead-thesis exit already embodies this; codify as an explicit risk rule so a mean_reversion expert never carries an atr_stop. Also relevant: mean-reversion strategies fail at maximum leverage after long winning streaks (LTCM-style overconfidence).
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Data errors inflate mean-reversion backtests and poison spread strategies; deflate momentum backtests
findings.mechanism: a single erroneous outlier price creates a fictitious entry at the bad level and a mean-reverting-looking return when price returns to truth; errors are large relative to small spreads
findings.setup_summary: An outlier (e.g., a bogus $110 print on a $100 stock) produces fictitious mean-reversion profit (short at 110, cover at 100) and fictitious momentum loss (buy at 110, stopped at 100) in backtests, and real losing trades in live execution when erroneous bid/ask quotes trigger orders. Spread and arbitrage strategies are most sensitive because the error is a large fraction of the small spread (a $1 error on a $5 spread is 20%). Currency venues especially: no regulation requires trade-price reporting; bid-ask spread varies by venue, so costs are venue-dependent.
findings.trigger_invalidation: N/A - data-quality gate for the V8 lab/data pipeline.
findings.risk_geometry: No trade geometry; data-cleaning requirement (exchange cancel-and-correct codes, primary-exchange prices, synchronized settlement prices for spreads).
findings.quote: If there are errors, or 'outliers,' in the historical data used for backtesting, then these errors usually inflate the backtest performance of mean-reverting strategies.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 3, 'The Danger of Data Errors' (see also Chapter 1 pitfalls: look-ahead, survivorship, primary vs consolidated, futures roll/settlement)
findings.notes: V8 lab/source-integrity rule: mean-reversion backtests are a canary for tape errors; re-run any z-score/band expert result with spike-filtered data. The pitfall taxonomy in Chapter 1 (look-ahead, survivorship, primary-vs-consolidated, futures close-vs-settlement, roll back-adjustment) is a checklist for the V8 data pipeline.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

findings.strategy_name: Buy-on-gap: seasonal intraday mean reversion with a momentum filter (reversion only when above the MA)
findings.mechanism: liquidity-demand selling at a session open overshoots and reverts, but only when the drop is not news-driven; the long-term-MA filter separates the two
findings.setup_summary: At market open, select stocks whose open is more than 1 std (90-day close-to-close) below the previous day's low (gapped down) AND whose open is above the 20-day moving average of closes; buy the 10 lowest, liquidate at the close. SPX backtest: APR 8.7%, Sharpe 1.5 (2006-2012). Mirror short version (gap up, below MA): APR 46%, Sharpe 1.27, steeper drawdown. Key transferable idea: price series that show no mean reversion on daily closes can show strong mean reversion in specific periods/sessions ('seasonal' or time-conditioned mean reversion); the momentum filter (price above a longer MA) keeps out drops caused by real news.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Open below the MA (news-driven drop, no reversion); panic selling does not finish intraday; open-close drift turns negative.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry at session open (uses preopen prices - signal noise acknowledged), exit at close; ~10 positions, intraday, no overnight.
findings.quote: on days when the stock index futures are down before the open, certain stocks suffer disproportionately due to panic selling at the open. But once this panic selling is over, the stock will gradually appreciate over the course of the day.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 4, 'Intraday Mean Reversion: Buy-on-Gap Model' (Example 4.1)
findings.notes: Crypto has no opening auction or exchange gaps (24/7), so the literal gap setup does not translate. The transferable lessons are (a) time-conditioned/seasonal mean reversion as a V8 time-of-day feature, and (b) the momentum-filter-on-mean-reversion technique that 'reprises often' in the book - a strong FEATURE_INPUT for the mean_reversion_band family.
findings.book: Algorithmic Trading - Winning Strategies and Their Rationale 2013

book_title: Algorithmic Trading: Winning Strategies and Their Rationale (Ernest P. Chan, 2013) — Part 1 of 2 (Chapters 1-7)
The Trend Following Bible (Part 1) - Andrew Abraham, Wiley 2013

findings.strategy_name: Donchian channel breakout with MACD momentum filter
findings.mechanism: price taking out the X-day channel extreme resumes the prior trend; smoothed-momentum and MACD filters screen out counter-trend/false breakouts
findings.setup_summary: Within a universe of markets ranked strongest/weakest by smoothed rate of change, buy a breakout above the X-day high (classic 20-day) when MACD is above zero and rising; short mirror on the Y-day low (10-day) when MACD below zero and falling. Pass the trade if the dollar risk from the X-day high to the Y-day low exceeds ~1% of core equity. Hard stop = Y-day low (longs).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Hard stop (Y-day low) touched = small loss, exit and take the next signal; MACD flipping against direction cancels pending breakout consideration and invalidates the higher-TF thesis.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: stop/close through X-day high (longs) or Y-day low (shorts); initial hard stop = Y-day low (long) / X-day high (short), set immediately at fill and not moved; once trade works, replace hard stop with 39-period ATR trailing stop; no profit target; no expiry beyond stops.
findings.quote: Donchian made it very simple: Buy the 20‐day high and sell the 10‐day low.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.6 'Your Complete Robust Trading Plan' Step 2; Ch.7 'Trend Breakouts'
findings.notes: Distinct from the backlog breakout_retest family (which is location/re-entry based): this is a pure channel-breakout continuation with a momentum regime gate. 24/7 crypto means no overnight gaps or limit-locks, so breakout and hard-stop orders fill exactly; high leverage makes the 1%-risk gate load-bearing; funding cost must be added to the simulator for multi-day holds. Book warns shorter X/Y params -> more false breakouts.
findings.book: The Trend Following Bible - How Professional Traders Compound Wealth and Manage Risk 2012

findings.strategy_name: Higher-timeframe trend retracement with 2-bar pullback stop entry
findings.mechanism: the higher timeframe defines the tradable trend; a lower-timeframe retracement against it is transient, creating a low-risk continuation entry once price resumes the higher-TF direction
findings.setup_summary: Weekly MACD positive and above zero (long setup) while the daily Elder Force / retracement oscillator crosses below zero (pullback); place a buy stop 1 tick (0.001%) above the high of the prior two bars and ratchet it lower each bar until filled or the weekly MACD reverses. Mirror for shorts. Hard stop = 1 tick below the two-bar low.
findings.trigger_invalidation: If not filled, re-place the stop at each new bar; cancel the stop when the higher-timeframe MACD reverses. Hard stop hit = exit; thesis invalid only when higher-TF trend (weekly MACD) flips.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: buy stop 1 tick above prior 2-bar high (long) / sell stop below prior 2-bar low (short); hard stop = 2-bar low (long); replace with trailing ATR stop once in open profit (hold hard stop until ATR stop is tighter); position size = (1% of core equity) / (entry minus 2-bar low).
findings.quote: We put in a buy stop one tick or .001 percent above the high of the prior two bars.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.8 'Trend Retracements' Steps 1-3 and 'Protect Yourself'
findings.notes: Book variant differs from the current V8 trend_pullback (ema_fast>ema_slow + next-bar-close entry): this one uses higher-TF MACD regime + two-bar pullback + intra-bar stop entry with ratchet. A candidate variant under the same family. Book explicitly rejects 1-bar stops as too whipsaw-prone ('too sensitive'). 24/7 markets make the ratchet continuous; no gaps simplify stop semantics.
findings.book: The Trend Following Bible - How Professional Traders Compound Wealth and Manage Risk 2012

findings.strategy_name: Smoothed rate-of-change universe ranking (trade only strongest/weakest)
findings.mechanism: relative strength persists: the strongest markets are most likely to keep trending higher and the weakest to keep falling, so the universe filter precedes the signal
findings.setup_summary: Rank every candidate market by the average of three rate-of-change periods (e.g., 2/5/7) computed on the higher timeframe (weekly), smoothed to remove spikes; take long candidates only from the strongest decile and short candidates only from the weakest, then apply the 1%-risk gate before entry.
findings.trigger_invalidation: A market falling out of the strong/weak ranking drops out of the candidate universe for new signals; open trades governed by stops, not by ranking.
findings.risk_geometry: Universe filter only — no change to entry/stop/target geometry; the author notes commodities need nominal adjustment and volume must be checked for liquidity.
findings.quote: I look to buy the strongest trending markets and look to sell the weakest trending markets.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.5 'Choose Markets to Reduce Risk' (ROC code listing)
findings.notes: This is a cross-sectional universe/feature filter, not a shared ranker scoring experts (V8 rule: ranker ABSENT by default). Degenerates to a single-market momentum check for a BTC-only system; becomes load-bearing if V8 expands across perp instruments. Book also adds 52-week and all-time new-high/new-low screens as universe inputs.
findings.book: The Trend Following Bible - How Professional Traders Compound Wealth and Manage Risk 2012

findings.strategy_name: ATR trailing stop replacing the hard structural stop
findings.mechanism: a volatility-scaled trailing stop protects open profit while giving the trade enough room to breathe through normal noise
findings.setup_summary: On entry, the hard stop is a structural extreme (Y-day low for longs). Once the trade moves in favor, switch to an ATR-based trailing stop (author prefers 39-period ATR on daily bars) placed a multiple of ATR from price that only moves in the trade's favor; hold the hard stop until the ATR stop is tighter. Trade ends when either stop is touched.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Exit only via the hard or trailing stop — the book explicitly accepts never exiting at highs/lows ('Only liars get out at the highs or lows').
findings.risk_geometry: Entry + initial stop structural (channel/swing extreme); trailing exit = multiple of 39-period ATR from price, ratcheting in favor; no profit target.
findings.quote: the ATR trailing stop is one way to limit losses and protect profits.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.6 'Stops' / 'If the Trade Starts Working' (True Range definition)
findings.notes: Maps directly to V8 risk_geometry's atr_ref, adding the explicit rule: switch from structural hard stop to ATR trailing stop only once the ATR stop is tighter than the hard stop. The book's own trading-plan question (touch vs close-through on the ATR stop) is exactly the kind of frozen decision V8 requires. No gaps in crypto make the trailing stop precise; funding adds carry that must be absorbed by the ATR multiple.
findings.book: The Trend Following Bible - How Professional Traders Compound Wealth and Manage Risk 2012

findings.strategy_name: Fixed-fractional 1% risk sizing on core equity
findings.mechanism: risking a constant small fraction of true closed equity per trade keeps any single loss survivable across the long runs of losers trend following produces
findings.setup_summary: Risk 0.75-1.25% of core equity (cash + closed positions, explicitly EXCLUDING open-trade profits) per trade. Position size = (cap% x core equity) / (entry minus hard-stop distance). Skip any trade whose computed risk exceeds the cap regardless of conviction.
findings.trigger_invalidation: N/A — a sizing/admission rule; the trade is skipped when risk % exceeds the cap.
findings.risk_geometry: Stop-based sizing: shares/contracts = (cap x core equity) / (entry - hard stop); core equity excludes open equity so a run-up cannot inflate position size.
findings.quote: you do not want to risk more than 1 percent of your account on any one trade.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.1 'Make Sure You Are Properly Funded'; Ch.5 'Risk per Trade' (worked examples)
findings.notes: The book gives worked sizing arithmetic (e.g., $1,000 risk / $3 stop = 333 shares) and the risk-of-ruin formula supporting the 1% heuristic. The core-equity (exclude open profits) definition is the load-bearing detail versus naive account-equity sizing and maps to V8's core-equity conventions.
findings.book: The Trend Following Bible - How Professional Traders Compound Wealth and Manage Risk 2012

findings.strategy_name: Sector risk cap (5% of portfolio per sector)
findings.mechanism: positions within one correlated sector are effectively one risk, so summing them understates true portfolio risk
findings.setup_summary: Cap aggregate risk allocated to any one sector (e.g., interest rates, grains, tech) at 5% of portfolio. Do not take a new trade if it would push that sector's summed risk above 5%. Sectors = correlated groups (gold->silver, soybeans->corn->wheat, tech shares).
findings.trigger_invalidation: N/A — an admission gate at portfolio level; a position may only open when the sector aggregate stays under the cap.
findings.risk_geometry: Aggregate-risk cap across correlated instruments; per-trade stops unchanged.
findings.quote: I will only allocate 5 percent of my total portfolio to any sector.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.5 'Risk per Sector'
findings.notes: Author's own blowup narrative (buying bonds across the whole curve = one correlated bet) grounds V8's 'one active exposure per (instrument, direction)' rule and any future altcoin expansion. Book notes the correlation coefficient is backward-looking and correlations change — so the cap is heuristic, not a fitted correlation model.
findings.book: The Trend Following Bible - How Professional Traders Compound Wealth and Manage Risk 2012

findings.strategy_name: Open-trade-equity heat cap (20% of core equity)
findings.mechanism: the portfolio's deepest drawdowns arrive right after the biggest open-profit run-ups, so exposure must be capped when open profits run hot
findings.setup_summary: Measure open-trade profits / core equity (cash + closed equity). When the ratio reaches 20%, stop taking any new positions until open equity subsides below the cap. Alternative lever: tighten the ATR stops or take partial profits.
findings.trigger_invalidation: New admissions resume only when the ratio drops below the cap.
findings.risk_geometry: Portfolio-level admission gate layered on per-trade stops; author states his biggest drawdowns follow his largest open-trade-profit periods.
findings.quote: I cap my total open trade equity versus my core equity at 20 percent of my core equity.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.5 'Overall Risk on the Portfolio'
