findings.risk_geometry: Entry at the mean-reversion price; stop = the adverse range boundary (book: boundaries are 'lines in the sand'); target = the opposite range boundary; expiry = forecast time the range persists (match the option expiry to projected range duration).
findings.quote: As soon as the price action proves the forecast for a directionless market to be incorrect by breaking through a key support or resistance level, one needs to exit the trade.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 5, 'Butterflies and Condors', 'Managing Risk and Taking Losses' (p. 153)
findings.notes: BTC 1h exhibits persistent bounded ranges and mean-reversion behavior; 24/7 trading means boundary breaks are clean close-bar signals with no closed-market gaps. Edge claim unproven - needs OOS falsification. Book profits the range via long butterfly/condor (short-vol wrapper with hard risk limit), which is not perp-executable, but the range-identification and invalidation framework transfers directly.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Consolidation-to-expansion volatility breakout (long straddle/strangle thesis)
findings.mechanism: tight consolidation precedes a large-magnitude move in either direction; profit comes from the expansion exceeding the premium paid, not from direction
findings.setup_summary: After a period of consolidation bounded by support/resistance, forecast a large-magnitude move away from the consolidation (the book's setup for long straddles/strangles). The magnitude must exceed the premium: breakevens are strike +/- debit. In perp terms: tight range compression followed by directional expansion; direction at entry is not required, only magnitude.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Entry after consolidation; thesis fails if no breakout occurs before the time stop (each day of no movement bleeds theta - 'death of a thousand cuts') or if the structure value breaches a preset price stop; breakevens at strike +/- premium define the magnitude the move must exceed.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry after consolidation at the strike; stops = BOTH a price stop on the structure and a time stop (a date beyond which the position is not carried); target = breakeven distance (strike +/- premium).
findings.quote: In this scenario, the trader of a long straddle or strangle should be looking for a large magnitude move (that is, a breakout) away from the strike price.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 4, 'Straddles and Strangles', 'Strategy Component Selection' (p. 119)
findings.notes: The straddle/strangle structure is not perp-executable, but the market-timing thesis (consolidation -> expansion) is the core of tight-range breakout trading and can feed the existing breakout_retest backlog family (range-compression entry, trend-expansion exit). Time-stop discipline is mandatory since perp funding/carry plays the theta role.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Dual time-stop + price-stop rule for carry-negative positions
findings.mechanism: positions that bleed carry every day must be bounded by the lesser of a price stop and a time stop - the clock is the enemy when carry is negative
findings.setup_summary: Risk rule: for any position with negative time/carry cost (book: long option premium; perp analog: paying funding, or holding a thesis that pays funding against you), quantify BOTH the price risk and the time risk before entry and exit when the lesser of the two is reached. Movement of the underlying works in the trader's favor; movement of the clock does not.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Exit when either the preset price stop or the preset time stop is hit, whichever comes first.
findings.risk_geometry: Dual stops defined at entry: price stop on the position and time stop (calendar date / bar count); exit on the lesser of the two.
findings.quote: It is important to set both price and time constraints on these types of positions. It is important to quantify the price risk and the time risk you are willing to take before the trade is made and exit when the lesser of the two is reached.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 4, 'Straddles and Strangles', 'Risk: Long Straddles and Strangles' (p. 120)
findings.notes: Directly transferable: V8 already carries expiry_bars in risk_geometry; this book corroborates the requirement that carry-negative positions get a time budget that is enforced independently of the price stop. Funding in perps plays the role of theta.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Assumption-invalidation lifecycle exit ('if you are wrong, get out')
findings.mechanism: every trade is a bundle of forecast assumptions; when any one is falsified by price, the position is dead and must be liquidated immediately
findings.setup_summary: Lifecycle rule: plan exits for every assumption BEFORE entry (direction, magnitude, volatility behavior, timing - 'what does one do if he is completely wrong on direction? what if volatility behavior... turn out to be incorrect?'). If any assumption proves wrong, liquidate immediately; no hoping or praying, and avoid the classic error of staying too long or over-modifying a position whose view has changed.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Any falsification of an original forecast assumption (wrong direction, wrong magnitude, wrong timing, wrong volatility behavior) triggers immediate exit; also exit when the forecast has been met (target reached).
findings.risk_geometry: Exits predefined at entry; when wrong, get out rather than modify repeatedly ('The simplest and most effective rule in risk management is this: If the trader is wrong, he should get out!').
findings.quote: The simplest and most effective rule in risk management is this: If the trader is wrong, he should get out!
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 2, 'Verticals', 'Trade Management' (p. 56)
findings.notes: Corroborates V8's still_valid / dead-thesis separation between stops and thesis invalidation. The rule is stated nearly verbatim across Chapters 2, 3, and 6, making it a load-bearing lifecycle invariant.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Profit-banking roll while maintaining directional exposure
findings.mechanism: as a winning directional trade progresses, periodically bank profit and reduce risk while keeping exposure in the direction of the move, then close fully when the move is judged over
findings.setup_summary: Lifecycle rule for the successful position: when the underlying moves in the forecast direction, manage the winner by periodically taking money off the table while maintaining exposure (in options, rolling the long leg via vertical spreads; in perps, scaling out / trailing). Rolling 'maintains the exposure in the direction of the breakout, reduces risk and takes money off the table, and puts the trader in a strong psychological position'. Close entirely as soon as the move appears over; never leave residual short/opposing legs open.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Continue rolling/scaling while the directional move persists; close fully when the trader feels the move is over or momentum fades; the short/opposite leg must be closed once the breakout is confirmed even if far OTM ('never... leave short option positions open, no matter how far out-of-the-money').
findings.risk_geometry: Roll/scaling points at momentum pauses; profit banked at each roll; final close when the move ends; keep stops on any remaining opposite leg. Extra execution costs from each adjustment reduce profit.
findings.quote: Rolling a long option position is an excellent way to manage a position that is 'going your way.' ... It maintains the exposure in the direction of the breakout. It reduces risk and takes 'money off the table.'
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 3, 'Collars and Reverse-Collars', 'Managing the Successful Position' (p. 86)
findings.notes: Directly applicable to trend-trade lifecycle: V8's position_scaling/break_even_stop vocabulary matches. The 'exit when the move is over' rule requires a momentum-based close signal (response feature group).
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Trigger-price (pivot) anchored breakout
findings.mechanism: a specific price level - the top/bottom of a consolidation - acts as the launch pad; the move only begins when price trades through the trigger
findings.setup_summary: Identify the trigger/pivot price - the level whose trade-through is expected to launch a large move (e.g., the top of a range, or a consolidation boundary). Anchor the long exposure at the trigger to capture most of the forecast move, and place the opposite-side short at significant resistance (collar) or support (reverse-collar). Choose an expiry that comfortably covers the forecast time horizon with margin (book example: consolidation historically lasted 10-15 days, so choose the 60-day expiry over the 28-day).
findings.trigger_invalidation: The trade is contingent on price trading through the trigger price; if the trigger is not reached by expiry the position 'fails to trigger' and must be rolled to the next cycle or closed. Stop-loss on the opposite short leg at the key support/resistance level, below which the forecast is wrong.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry anchored at the trigger price; short-leg stop at significant resistance (collar) or support (reverse-collar); expiry = forecast time horizon plus buffer; cost kept near zero by choosing equidistant strikes.
findings.quote: ABC is trapped in a range between 100.00 and 105.00. The trader believes that the next time it trades through 105.00 ABC is going to break out for a large upside move. In this case 105.00 is the trigger price. (In technical analysis lingo, this is sometimes referred to as the pivot price.)
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 3, 'Collars and Reverse-Collars', 'What Is the Trigger Price of the Forecast Move?' (p. 82)
findings.notes: The trigger/pivot anchoring is the structural core of breakout trading and feeds the existing breakout_retest / failed_breakout location logic. The expiry-with-margin rule transfers as a time-horizon buffer. The collar structure itself is not perp-executable.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: 'Rate of return is a trap' - yield is risk compensation, not edge
findings.mechanism: premium/carry yield is the market's price for perceived risk, not a standalone edge; elevated yield only signals that participants expect larger moves
findings.setup_summary: Methodology lesson: never select an income/premium-selling strategy on the basis of its rate of return or premium yield alone. The rate of return is 'simply an indicator of the risk level perceived by market participants' - high premiums mean participants have built in the possibility of larger moves. The underlying price forecast must be the first determining factor. Direct perp analog: do not select funding-carry trades purely because funding is high; the carry is compensation for the directional and liquidation risk the market prices in.
findings.trigger_invalidation: N/A - methodology lesson applying at strategy-selection stage, not trade entry; governs whether a carry/premium trade is even admissible given a market view.
findings.risk_geometry: N/A - methodology; shapes selection and sizing, not entry/stop geometry.
findings.quote: It is the neutral to bullish price forecast that should be the first determining factor for a covered-write, never the rate of return! The rate of return is simply an indicator of the risk level perceived by market participants at that time. Using rate of return to determine covered-write strategies is a trap.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 1, 'The Covered-Write', 'What Is the Current State of Implied Volatility in the Market?' (p. 19)
findings.notes: Load-bearing for V8's carry/funding work: prevents promoting funding_carry or premium-collection as standalone edge. Corroborated by Chapter 7's warning that 'implied volatility differentials in and of themselves usually are not sufficient reason to initiate a ratio spread.'
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Sell-the-rich-side volatility skew structuring
findings.mechanism: when implied volatilities differ across strikes, express a directional/neutral view by selling the high-IV leg and buying the low-IV leg
findings.setup_summary: Feature/structuring rule: implied volatilities differ by strike (the skew/'smirk'/'smile'), with lower-strike options typically at higher IV. When the skew is steep, a bullish trader can make a reverse-collar more attractive because the put being sold carries much higher IV than the call being bought - selling the rich leg and buying the cheap leg adds a structuring 'edge'. A flat skew can make the bearish collar attractive for the same reason. The differential alone is never a sufficient reason to trade.
findings.trigger_invalidation: A skew differential only structures a trade that already has a directional or range forecast; a differential without a market view is insufficient. Trade only when both conditions hold.
findings.risk_geometry: Sell the high-IV side, buy the low-IV side; standard stop-loss discipline on the short leg at key levels.
findings.quote: If the market demonstrates a large implied volatility skew, sometimes a reverse-collar trade becomes more appetizing to the bullish trader because the implied volatility of the put option being sold could be much higher than the implied volatility of the call option being bought, giving the trader an additional 'edge' to work with.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 3, 'Collars and Reverse-Collars', 'Implied Volatility Skew' (p. 84)
findings.notes: Perps have no options IV, so the direct analog is funding-rate asymmetry / skew (enter the side that receives funding when funding is extreme) - candidate input for a funding-skew feature and for structuring direction on funding-rich sides. Chapter 7 repeats the principle for ratio spreads as 'buy-low-volatility-strike, sell-high-volatility-strike' skew plays.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Synthetic-equivalency relative-value arbitrage (box / jelly roll) as basis analog
findings.mechanism: synthetically equivalent exposures must price to the same fair value; persistent deviation reveals a relative-value edge that converges at expiry
findings.setup_summary: Relative-value methodology: the long box (bull call spread + bear put spread, same strikes/expiry) has zero Greeks and a maturity value of the strike differential discounted by carry, so call-spread value + put-spread value must equal box value; the jelly roll anchors call vs put time spreads to a carry differential. 'If the equation does not balance, there is a relative advantage available' - pick the cheap synthetic for entry or exit. Perp analog: perp-vs-spot basis and funding deviations from fair value create cash-and-carry / basis convergence trades.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Enter only when the identity (CS+PS=BOX; CTS-PTS=JR) is out of balance beyond execution costs; exit on convergence to fair value. Execution costs (commissions, wide ITM spreads) can erase the edge.
findings.risk_geometry: Market-neutral structure with zero delta/gamma/vega/theta; risk = carry, execution cost, and expiry handling; needs spot+perp data (DATA_BLOCKED until derivatives tape in V8).
findings.quote: Remember that call spread value + put spread value = box value. If the equation does not balance, there is a relative advantage available.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 2, 'Verticals', 'Practical Uses' (p. 54)
findings.notes: The box/jelly-roll identities are the equity-option form of the perp basis/carry identity (funding_present_value + spot = perp). For V8 this is a backlog family gated on the derivatives tape; the methodology lesson (relative-value entry/exit selection) transfers even before the tape exists as an execution principle.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Volatility term-structure regime (short-dated spikes, long-dated tracks history)
findings.mechanism: short-dated implied volatility spikes on volatile periods and collapses on quiet periods while long-dated IV tracks historical volatility, creating a term-structure shape that selects long vs short time-spread strategies
findings.setup_summary: Feature input: implied volatility levels generally differ across expiration cycles (the term structure). After a slow period, near-term IV is depressed relative to long-dated (upward slope) - favoring short time spreads (sell the rich far-dated); after a volatile period, near-term IV is elevated (downward slope) - favoring long time spreads (buy the cheaper far-dated, sell the rich near-dated). The term structure must align with a price/time forecast; it is not sufficient to justify a trade on its own.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Term structure must align with a price/time forecast to warrant a trade; a pure term-structure signal is insufficient (corroborates the 'yield is a trap' lesson).
findings.risk_geometry: Long time spread: buy far-dated, sell near-dated at target strike; positive theta + long vega, risk limited to debit; short time spread is the reverse (positive gamma, short vega) but carries unquantifiable short-side risk through the near expiry.
findings.quote: The implied volatility of short-dated options will conform to short-term events, spiking when underlying price movement is volatile, collapsing when it is not, whereas the longer-dated options will trade more in line with the historical long-term volatility.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 6, 'Calendar Spreads', 'Implied Volatility Differentials' (p. 174)
findings.notes: For perps the analog is short-window vs long-window realized-volatility divergence plus the funding-rate term structure - a regime classifier input for gating volatility-sensitive families (e.g., run mean-reversion/range trades in the collapsed-vol regime, favor expansion plays after vol compression).
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: No-free-lunch cost-side accounting (gamma/theta/vega symmetry)
findings.mechanism: every convexity or carry advantage carries a symmetric cost - long-gamma pays theta and bleeds on IV decline; short-gamma collects theta but carries unlimited move/IV-spike tail risk
findings.setup_summary: Methodology lesson: strategies that appear to profit from the mere passage of time (short premium: 'what could be more certain than time passing?') or from movement in every direction (long premium) carry a mirrored cost. Long-gamma positions pay theta every day and are exposed to IV declines ('death of a thousand cuts'); short-gamma positions are exposed to large moves and IV spikes that can wipe out accumulated time-decay income in one bar. The cost side must be quantified and factored into the forecast before the trade.
findings.trigger_invalidation: N/A - methodology lesson; informs position sizing, regime gating, and the decision to carry versus exit; applies before entry.
findings.risk_geometry: Cost-side budgeting at selection; the theta/gamma mirror images (Figures 4.10 and 4.12) imply time-based discipline for convexity longs and hard stops for convexity shorts.
findings.quote: The bottom line is that there is no free lunch with straddles and strangles. For every upside there is a downside, and the risks have to be understood, factored into the forecast, and properly managed in a disciplined fashion.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 4, 'Straddles and Strangles', 'Risk and Reward, There Is No Free Lunch!' (p. 122)
findings.notes: Directly relevant to V8's funding-carry and carry-negative experts: perp funding plays the theta role, so a long-position-paying-funding thesis must budget carry the same way the book budgets theta, and a funding-collecting thesis must budget the liquidation/expansion tail.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Stop-loss semantics differ in 24/7 markets (closed-market gap risk vanishes)
findings.mechanism: equities stop-losses give no protection when the market is closed and gaps can run through stops; 24/7 perp trading removes closed-market gap risk, changing the stop-loss risk profile
findings.setup_summary: Methodology lesson: the book repeatedly warns that stop-loss orders 'do not provide any guarantees for how and when they will be executed, and they provide no coverage when the market is closed' and that news can gap price through a stop level. In 24/7 crypto perps the closed-market gap window is structurally absent, so stop-losses on bar-close/limit fills behave differently from the book's equities model; the residual tail risks are liquidation cascades, funding shocks, and exchange outages rather than overnight gaps.
findings.trigger_invalidation: N/A - methodology affecting risk-rule and simulator calibration (the V8 simulator's gap semantics should model 24/7 continuous trading, not equity-style overnight gaps).
findings.risk_geometry: Stops execute continuously; sizing must still account for liquidation cascades and leverage-triggered waterfall moves that take the place of gap risk.
findings.quote: All traders should keep in mind that stop-loss orders do not provide any guarantees for how and when they will be executed, and they provide no coverage when the market is closed.
findings.chapter_anchor: Chapter 3, 'Collars and Reverse-Collars', 'What Is the Trader's Risk Appetite?' (p. 85)
findings.notes: Also relevant to the book's Chapter 2 earnings-gap example (gap 30->37) - in perps an equivalent news move would trade through the stop continuously, so the failure mode shifts to cascade/liquidation; this should inform V8 risk_rule calibration and the simulator's gap/cost model.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

book_title: The Complete Turtle Trader (Covel, 2007) — Part 1

findings.strategy_name: Turtle Donchian Channel Breakout (S1 20-day / S2 55-day)
findings.mechanism: A market making a new N-day high/low has sufficient momentum that the trend tends to persist; follow it and exit when the opposite channel breaks.
findings.setup_summary: On BTCUSDT 1h, enter LONG when close makes a new 20-bar (System One) or 55-bar (System Two) high; enter SHORT on a new 20/55-bar low. Exit on the opposite-direction 10-bar (S1) or 20-bar (S2) breakout, or on the 2N stop, whichever triggers first. No target, no retracement waiting — buy the breakout at market.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: close makes new 20/55-bar channel extreme. Invalidated when price makes an opposite-direction 10/20-bar breakout (exit) or touches the 2N stop.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry next bar open (book: 'entry on the next trading day'); stop = 2N (2×20-day ATR); no R-multiple target, exit is structure-based (opposite channel breakout) or 2N stop; no fixed expiry — position held while trend persists.
findings.quote: System Two was the Turtles' longer-term trading system. It used an eleven-week breakout (fifty-five days) for an entry signal and a four-week breakout (twenty days) in the opposite direction for an exit.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'The Rules' (pp. 72-73)
findings.notes: Canonical trend-following family, distinct from existing V8 trend_pullback (EMA-cross entry) and failed_breakout (liquidity_vacuum). 24/7 perp tape has no exchange gaps so channel highs/lows are well-defined; funding cost is the main drag on an always-in-market breakout system. Candidate to formalize after the active 3 experts are screened; shares the 'trend_continuation' mechanism family with trend_pullback.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: 2N ATR Hard Stop (touch-based exit)
findings.mechanism: Sizing the stop to 2× daily volatility normalizes loss across markets and regimes so a stop-out costs roughly the same amount of risk every time.
findings.setup_summary: Place the primary hard stop at entry ± 2N, where N = 20-day average of true range (max of high-low, |high-prev close|, |low-prev close|). Exit when the stop price is touched — no second-guessing, no bar-close confirmation.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: price trades through the 2N stop level. Invalidated: none — the stop is unconditional and mechanical.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry-dependent stop distance = 2N (2×ATR) behind entry; STOP_FIRST touch semantics (matches V8 simulator); combined with the opposite-channel breakout as the second exit, whichever hits first.
findings.quote: The Turtles used a 2N stop. This simply means that their primary stop, or hard stop, was two times the daily 'N.' ... You would exit if the stop at price level $236 was 'touched.' No second-guessing. No overthinking. Follow the rules.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'The Rules', Risk Management (p. 84)
findings.notes: Refines existing V8 stop conventions (current experts use stop_r 1.0 with atr_ref): Turtle used 2×ATR and touch-based exit. Directly implementable as a RiskGate/risk_geometry rule; ATR (N) already exists in the volatility feature group.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Volatility-Scaled Unit Sizing (2% risk per unit)
findings.mechanism: Equalizing each unit's dollar risk to a fixed fraction of equity (2%) makes every market/position comparable and keeps drawdown survivable while waiting for the rare large trend.
findings.setup_summary: Size each unit so risk = 2% of current equity; contracts = (2% × equity) / (2N × contract value), rounded down to whole contracts. A 'unit' is the same risk in every market (one corn unit = one gold unit = one BTC unit).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Unit size recomputed daily from current equity and current N (volatility). No invalidation — continuous position-sizing rule.
findings.risk_geometry: Sizing rule only: fraction-of-equity risk (2%), volatility-normalized via 2N dollar risk, round down; cap 4-5 units per market.
findings.quote: They bet a fixed 2 percent of their capital on hand on each trade. If they had $100,000, they would bet (or risk) 2 percent ($2,000) on each trade. Each 2 percent bet of their equity was called a 'unit.'
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'The Rules', Risk Management (pp. 83-86)
findings.notes: Core position-sizing risk rule for V8's RiskGate. On leveraged perps this is the mechanism that prevents liquidation-driven ruin: risk per unit is defined as fraction-of-equity, not contract count. Rounding down and daily N update are directly mechanizable.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Turtle Pyramiding (add units at 1N intervals, stop ratchet)
findings.mechanism: Reinforcing winners compounds the payoff of the rare big trend; ratcheting stops to the newest unit's 2N protects accumulated open profit without exiting early.
findings.setup_summary: After a breakout entry, add one unit at each favorable 1N move (entry+1N, +2N, ...) up to a maximum of 5 units. Stops: 1/2N on the first trading day, then 2N thereafter; each time a unit is added, all stops are brought up to that newest unit's 2N stop (break-even ratchet).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger to add: price moves 1N in trade direction. All stops ride the newest unit's 2N; if the ratcheted stop is hit the whole position exits.
findings.risk_geometry: Adds at +1N intervals, max 5 units; stop = 1/2N day one, then 2N behind the newest add; no R-multiple target — exit by stop or opposite-channel breakout; total risk to original equity is bounded by 2% per unit added.
findings.quote: A new unit will be added at 105, 110, etc. Turtles could pyramid a maximum of 5 units. They set their stops at ½N on the first day of trading and from that point forward, 2N stops were used. Then, once the second unit was bought, both stops were brought up to the new unit's 2N stop.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'The Rules', Pyramiding (pp. 87-91)
findings.notes: Position-scaling lifecycle behavior for V8's ExposureBook. Currently V8 holds ONE exposure per (instrument,direction); pyramiding is a scaling variant to test later against the single-unit baseline. On perps the 2N stop must account for liquidation price, so heat per added unit needs explicit modeling.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Drawdown-Scaled De-Risking (20% unit cut per 10% DD)
findings.mechanism: Reducing unit size arithmetically during drawdowns counters the exponential path toward ruin and preserves capital so a recovery trend can be captured with full size restored.
findings.setup_summary: For every 10% equity drawdown from peak, cut unit risk by 20% (2.0% -> 1.6% -> 1.28% ...). Restore unit size progressively as equity recovers. Example: down 11% -> trade 1.6% units; down 22% -> 1.28% units.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: account drawdown crosses each 10% threshold. Rule reverses (re-increase) only when equity starts recovering toward peak.
findings.risk_geometry: Equity-based position de-leveraging ladder; a pure risk-management overlay on top of the entry/exit system.
findings.quote: For every 10 percent in drawdown in their account, Turtles cut their trading unit risk by 20 percent. ... If their trading capital dropped down 22 percent, then they would cut their trading size by another 20 percent (1.6 × 80%), making each unit 1.28 percent.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'The Rules', Risk of Ruin (pp. 92-93)
findings.notes: Directly portable to V8's RiskGate as a drawdown-scaled sizing ladder. Especially important under perp leverage where drawdowns accelerate via liquidation; the rule is falsifiable (compare fixed-2% vs de-leveraged sizing on the same tape).
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Correlation Cap and Long/Short Unit Netting
findings.mechanism: Correlated markets act as one big position; capping per-market units and netting long vs short units keeps true portfolio risk at the intended level.
findings.setup_summary: Limit 4-5 units in any one market and avoid stacking highly correlated markets (gold+silver, Dow+S&P count as one position). Total portfolio unit risk is computed as larger − (smaller/2) between long and short unit totals, which allows more units overall while keeping risk constant.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Portfolio-construction rule evaluated at position-sizing time; prevents unit-limit breach rather than invalidating a trade.
findings.risk_geometry: Portfolio-level cap: per-market unit limit (4-5), correlated-market avoidance, long/short netting formula total_risk = max(L,S) − min(L,S)/2.
findings.quote: Too many potentially correlated markets in a portfolio and the Turtles increased their unit risk. ... To calculate the total Turtle unit risk, you would take the smaller number and divide it by two. Then you would subtract that number from the larger number.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'The Rules', Portfolio Selection and Position Balancing (pp. 94-97)
findings.notes: For V8's current single-instrument (BTCUSDT) scope the cross-market correlation cap is latent; the long/short netting math becomes relevant if the instrument universe expands. The per-market unit cap maps to V8's heat cap / one-exposure rule.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: System One Winner-Skip Filter (take breakouts after losses)
findings.mechanism: Breakout signals cluster: consecutive breakouts after a winning one are disproportionately false, while a breakout taken after a prior loss is more likely the real trend; S2 is the fail-safe for filtered-out moves.
findings.setup_summary: Skip a 20-day (S1) breakout if the previous 20-day breakout signal was a winner (even if it was not taken); do take it if the previous signal ended in a 2N loss. The 55-day (S2) breakout remains mandatory and catches big trends the filter skipped.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: new 20-day breakout; filter uses outcome of the prior 20-day breakout signal. A skipped S1 breakout that keeps trending is re-entered on the S2 55-day breakout.
findings.risk_geometry: Signal-selection filter only, no change to stop/target geometry; S2 entry is the fail-safe re-entry path.
findings.quote: The Turtles ignored the System One four-week breakout signal if the last four-week breakout signal was a winner. ... if the trade before a current four-week breakout was a 2N loss, they could take the breakout.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'The Rules', System One and System Two (p. 72)
findings.notes: Requires a 'prior signal outcome' feature (history feature group) tracking last breakout direction and result in N terms. Note the same book reports false breakouts are common (the Turtles accepted small losses on most breakouts), so the filter's edge is an empirical claim to test on crypto 1h, not a given.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Liquidations More Important Than Initiations (random-entry principle)
findings.mechanism: Trade payoff is determined primarily by the exit/liquidation criterion; entry has little information value once risk is controlled, so effort should go into exit design, not entry precision.
findings.setup_summary: Falsifiable claim: a system with random/near-random entries and a disciplined liquidation rule (2N stop + opposite-channel breakout) performs surprisingly well. Entry price should not anchor any subsequent decision (trade as if you don't know your entry price).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Test: compare random-entry + Turtle exits vs Turtle breakouts + Turtle exits on the same tape; if random-entry performs near-equivalently, entry research is low-value for V8.
findings.risk_geometry: No entry geometry; the rule re-allocates research weight to exit/lifecycle design.
findings.quote: Our research indicated that liquidations are vastly more important than initiations. If you initiate purely randomly, you do surprisingly well with a good liquidation criterion.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'The Rules', Random Entries (p. 79)
findings.notes: Bears directly on V8's research allocation: exits, stops, and lifecycle (still_valid) dominate performance. Corroborates Eckhardt's memoryless-trading principle (Ch. 4) that entry price must not influence later decisions.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Expectation/Edge Metric (E = PW·AW − PL·AL)
findings.mechanism: Win rate is near-meaningless; edge is driven by the magnitude asymmetry of winners vs losers, so a low-win-rate system can have a far higher per-trade expectation than a high-win-rate one.
findings.setup_summary: Evaluate any V8 expert by edge E = (PW × AW) − (PL × AL). The book's data shows Turtle-style trend traders (35-40% winners, expectation 0.81-2.83 monthly) beat buy-and-hold index expectations (0.60-0.93). A system with 40% winners and $1000 avg win / $350 avg loss has edge $190 vs $75 for a 50%-winner system.
findings.trigger_invalidation: E > 0 required to trade; E is recomputed on frozen OOS per V8's learning protocol. Percent accuracy alone must never gate an expert.
findings.risk_geometry: Evaluation metric, not a trade geometry.
findings.quote: Edge = (PW × AW) − (PL × AL) ... The second trading system's 'edge' is 2.5 times that of the first even though it has a much lower winning percent. ... Percent accuracy means nothing.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'The Rules', Expectation (pp. 68-70)
findings.notes: Adopt E as the canonical per-trade metric for V8 registry/screening decisions (alongside drawdown and risk-of-ruin), replacing win-rate heuristics. The Turtle-vs-index expectation tables are a falsifiable empirical exhibit that magnitude asymmetry, not accuracy, is the driver.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Mean Reversion Tail Risk (LTCM/Amaranth caution)
findings.mechanism: Mean-reversion/arbitrage strategies are right most of the time and then suffer a fat-tail event where the market refuses to revert, wiping out years of small wins (LTCM 1998, Amaranth 2006).
findings.setup_summary: Caution against mean-reversion families: 'mean reversion works almost all of the time, then it stops and you're out of business.' Trend following accepts many small losses to be present for the rare large trend; Dennis/Turtles were net winners in August 1998 while LTCM imploded.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not a trade rule but a family-level gate: any mean-reversion expert must be stress-tested on regimes where the reversion thesis fails (trending/cascading markets), and sized so the failure scenario is survivable.
findings.risk_geometry: None — portfolio/philosophy-level constraint on which mechanism families V8 should prioritize.
findings.quote: Mean reversion works almost all of the time. Then it stops and you're kind of out of business. The market is always reverting to the mean except when it doesn't.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 11 'Seizing Opportunity', Hedge Fund Blowups (p. 164)
findings.notes: Crypto perps are prone to funding-driven mean reversion with violent deleveraging cascades; this lesson argues for gating any mean-reversion family on tail-risk survival. Supports V8's trend-following orientation without claiming edge.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Parameter Robustness (minor changes must not matter)
findings.mechanism: A robust systematic rule's performance is flat across small parameter variations; if a one-day change in breakout length changes results materially, the system is fragile and overfit.
findings.setup_summary: Use robustness as the acceptance test for V8 experts and their variants: changing S1 entry from 20 to 21 bars (or a parameter by ~5%) must not materially change OOS performance. If it does, reject the parameterization as overfit. The core edge was attributed to simple breakout/moving-average components (Parker: 'two-thirds of that is what drives our profits').
findings.trigger_invalidation: A variant that passes on one parameter value but fails a neighborhood of values is quarantined as overfit rather than promoted.
findings.risk_geometry: Design/test methodology for expert variants; interacts with V8's variant multiplicity rules.
findings.quote: In reality, a minor change of a variable in any robust trading system should not cause significant performance changes. If it does, you are in trouble.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'The Rules' (p. 74)
findings.notes: Directly actionable for V8's variant discipline: parameter/threshold changes are variants of one family, and this rule supplies the acceptance criterion (performance plateau, not point estimate). Mirrors the book's warning against fixating on '20 vs 21 days'.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Money Abstraction and Memoryless Trading (N-units not dollars)
findings.mechanism: Anchoring to dollars, past entry prices, or prior equity distorts decisions; trading in volatility units (N) and treating equity as a current-state variable keeps the trader on the rules.
findings.setup_summary: Rule-adherence doctrine: think 'I have a half-unit on' not '$34M in bonds'; risk 2% of CURRENT equity (never of peak or original); never average down on a losing position ('adding to a loser is putting your hand back on the stove'); re-enter after a stop-out if the signal re-fires (Paul Tudor Jones re-entered 10 times before the trend paid).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not a tradable rule — a determinism/psychology guardrail. Violations (discretionary adds, vendetta re-entry in the same losing market, averaging down) are the behaviors V8's mechanical pipeline eliminates by construction.
findings.risk_geometry: None — behavioral constraint; operationalized in V8 as no wall-clock dependence, frozen refs, and dead-thesis (still_valid) exits.
findings.quote: You shouldn't care about how you got to the current state but rather about what you should do now. A trader who trades differentially because of swings in confidence is focusing on his or her own past rather than on current realities.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 4 'The Philosophy' (p. 58); losses/vendetta (pp. 60-62)
findings.notes: The behavioral failure modes the Turtles were trained against (averaging down, revenge re-entry, entry-price anchoring, funny-money on profits) are exactly the discretionary risks V8 removes via deterministic rules, frozen refs, and single-exposure lifecycle. Also: the discretionary S3 'flair account' was canned within ~6 weeks — supportive evidence for REJECT_FOR_V8 on discretionary sub-accounts.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

book_title: The Complete Turtle Trader: The Legend, the Lessons, the Results (Michael W. Covel, 2007)

findings.strategy_name: Cross-sectional relative strength (buy strongest, sell weakest)
findings.mechanism: Relative strength persists: the strongest market keeps outperforming while the weak one lags; fading the spread assumes a convergence that trend followers reject.
findings.setup_summary: Over a rolling window, rank a basket of markets/assets by return; when asset A clearly outperforms asset B in the same complex (Walsh's example: beans up 10c, corn down 5c), go LONG the strongest and SHORT the weakest; hold while the relative-strength ordering persists. Falsifiable on any cross-asset basket at daily bars.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Thesis dies when the relative-strength ordering flips or the spread collapses to zero; long leg starts underperforming the short leg.
findings.risk_geometry: Book states only the entry logic and direction; stop/target not given. V8 would need its standard ATR stop, R-multiple target, expiry_bars, and frozen relative-strength refs.
findings.quote: If beans are up 10 cents and corn is down five cents, we buy beans. Some people think to buy corn because it's going to catch up with beans. We take the opposite. We'd rather buy the commodity that's strongest and sell the one that's weakest.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.13 'Second-Generation Turtles', Mark J. Walsh (pp.172-173)
findings.notes: Requires a cross_market feature group (ranked momentum across instruments) which V8 does not yet have; single-instrument experts cannot express this. Cross-sectional momentum across crypto perps is testable on 24/7 data but majors are highly correlated and the short leg pays funding, so the spread edge is thinner than in commodities.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: New N-period high/low breakout trend entry ('buy the all-time high')
findings.mechanism: trend_continuation: a market printing prices never seen before is treated as a confirmed trend, not overextension, because the empirical frequency favors continuation over exhaustion.
findings.setup_summary: When close exceeds the highest high (or breaks the lowest low) of the prior N periods, enter with the trend at next bar; Abraham's version buys all-time-high regimes that make intuitive sellers uncomfortable. Falsifiable: does a new-window-high close predict continuation over the next M bars vs. random entries?
findings.trigger_invalidation: Close trades back through the breakout reference level -> failed breakout; abort or flip thesis (interfaces with the failed_breakout family).
findings.risk_geometry: Book restates no S1/S2 numbers in this part (those are in Part 1). V8 geometry: entry NEXT_BAR_CLOSE, stop 2xATR below entry or below breakout ref, target R-multiple, expiry_bars per system variant.
findings.quote: To buy crude oil at $55? That's a hard bet to do when it's never been to $56. Never in the history of the world has it been to $56 and you say, 'It hit $55 today, I'm buying it.'
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.13, Salem Abraham (p.184)
findings.notes: Distinct from the existing trend_pullback (which buys pullbacks inside an uptrend) and from the DATA_BLOCKED breakout_retest (which requires a retest). The specific donchian 20/55-day variants (S1/S2) belong to Part 1 under donchian_breakout; this finding is the generic new-high breakout concept. 24/7 crypto has no exchange gaps, so breakout entries are clean on BTCUSDT 1h.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: ATR-unit fixed-fractional sizing with disciplined leverage cap
findings.mechanism: Position size is set so each unit risks a fixed fraction of equity (scaled by ATR/N) and total portfolio leverage is capped so survival outranks return maximization.
findings.setup_summary: Size each trade so risk equals a fixed fraction of equity (one unit ~ 1% of equity per N); when drawdowns or volatility demand it, cut gross leverage (Dennis's 50% leverage-cut memo and Crocker's 'back off the leverage' both assert this). Abraham's rule of thumb: 'never going past 30' even though the vehicle allows 160.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Standing rule, not a trade setup; governs all positions continuously.
findings.risk_geometry: Book (this part) asserts the leverage-cap principle; stop = 2N from entry and unit = 1%-of-equity-per-N are Part 1 details. V8: map to RiskGate admission + heat cap.
findings.quote: If you make 30 percent a year, people will beat a path to your door. You need to back off on the leverage.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.13, Commodities Corporation meeting (p.182); leverage memo referenced in Ch.14 (p.188)
findings.notes: With perp leverage up to 100x, ATR-based fractional sizing is the primary risk control; the leverage-reduction-on-stress rule is a lifecycle signal (cut heat, not the system).
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Ruin-avoidance bet-size cap ('never bet the ranch')
findings.mechanism: Even with positive expectation, a position sized so a tail loss zeroes the account is unacceptable; the utility cost of ruin outweighs any edge.
findings.setup_summary: For any candidate trade with win-probability p and a full-stake loss on failure, refuse stake sizes that can wipe out equity regardless of edge (Abraham's coin-flip: 90% chance to double $10M, 10% chance to lose all -> still must decline). Standing constraint on per-trade and portfolio risk.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Standing rule; applies to every position continuously.
findings.risk_geometry: Per-trade risk must be a small fraction of equity even at worst-case (stop + liquidation gap); no R-multiple stated in the book beyond the principle.
findings.quote: If the upside is $10 million, the downside is $10 million . . . I've seen guys around here in Texas oil and gas businesses and they go broke. They're great oil and gas guys, but they bet the ranch too many times and lost it.
findings.chapter_anchor: Appendix I 'Where Are They Now?', Salem Abraham (p.191)
findings.notes: Perp liquidation makes ruin a concrete tail; add an explicit ruin constraint (never risk >k% of equity on one exposure) to RiskGate alongside the existing heat cap.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Tail-event protection ('what can never happen can happen')
findings.mechanism: tail_risk_conservatism: markets occasionally print multi-standard-deviation moves (Eurodollar +250 = ~10+ sigma in Oct 1987); stops and sizing must assume such moves occur intraday.
findings.setup_summary: Standing design assumption: extreme multi-sigma gaps are possible at any time; place stops with a gap/liquidation buffer and size so a 10+ sigma adverse move is survivable (Abraham's $66k halved to $33k and survived). Simulator must model gap-through-stop fills, not just next-bar-close fills.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Standing assumption; not a trade setup.
findings.risk_geometry: stop distance plus worst-case slippage such that the account survives an extreme adverse move; the book reports the actual halving, not a formula.
findings.quote: The one lesson I was clear on: always know the thing that they say can never happen, can happen.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.13, October 1987 crash (pp.179-180)
findings.notes: Directly informs simulator gap semantics: in leveraged 24/7 crypto, liquidation cascades can move price far beyond a stop within one bar; canonical L1 STOP_FIRST/fill-at-close must be stress-tested for gap-through-stop.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Distinguish volatility from risk (tail blowups hide under low vol)
findings.mechanism: tail_risk_measurement: using volatility/standard deviation as the risk measure misprices strategies whose real risk is a rare catastrophic tail; 'works 95% of the time' strategies are exactly the ones that blow up.
findings.setup_summary: When evaluating any candidate (strategy, expert, or portfolio), measure risk by drawdown path and fat-tail/liquidation exposure, not by vol alone; reject candidates whose 95% window hides a ruin tail.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Evaluation principle, not a trade setup.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated; the point is that vol-based risk geometry misprices tail risk.
findings.quote: The biggest single problem with these allocators is they completely confuse volatility and standard deviation with 'risk.' The two are completely noncorrelated. They want Amaranth, Long Term Capital Management . . . and that's going to work 95 percent of the time, but when it doesn't, they're broke.
findings.chapter_anchor: Appendix I, Jim DiMaria (pp.192-193)
findings.notes: Guidance for V8 registry gates and OOS evaluation: report tail metrics (max DD, liquidation-path stress), not only mean/variance, when screening challengers.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Systematic rule execution over discretion ('rules beat judgment')
findings.mechanism: rule_based_execution: a hired hand forced to follow exact rules outperforms a discretionary expert relying on intuition; teachable process dominates innate skill.
findings.setup_summary: Encode the strategy fully as rules and execute them exactly, with no discretion; the transferability claim is that any operator following the exact rules matches or beats the originator.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not a trade setup; it is the thesis that rule-adherence (not judgment) drives the track record.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated.
findings.quote: I think I could take a kid who wasn't my son and say, 'Do this, I'll pay you $50,000 a year, or you're fired if you don't exactly follow it.' He'd beat me every day, every week, every month and every year.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.14 'Model Greatness' epigraph, Tom Willis (p.187)
findings.notes: Validates V8's architecture (behavior families as fully specified falsifiable rule sets, no discretion in replay); no new strategy.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Bet on measured frequencies over theory ('trade the numbers')
findings.mechanism: evidence_over_narrative: when observed frequency (65% heads over 1M flips) contradicts accepted theory, bet with the empirical frequency; profits come from price-action statistics, not explanations.
findings.setup_summary: Research decision rule: prefer point-in-time measured frequencies over prior/theory when they conflict; a strategy survives only on frozen-OOS statistics, not on whether the mechanism is understood.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not a trade setup.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated.
findings.quote: Just because I don't understand it doesn't mean I'm not going to bet on it.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.13, Salem Abraham (p.184); Eckhardt: 'These are the odds; it's all a math game.' (p.183)
findings.notes: This is essentially the V8 charter (falsification over narrative, registry-gated evidence); reinforces the frozen-OOS and evidence-label rules rather than adding a strategy.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Trend-following payoff profile: long flat/down stretches punctuated by rare large gains
findings.mechanism: skew_expectation: trend systems have right-skewed monthly returns - most months small losses, occasional explosive trend months, and multi-year flat/down stretches - all inside long-horizon compounders.
findings.setup_summary: Design expectation backed by the book's published 19-20 year CFTC-filed tables (Parker, Abraham, Shanks, DiMaria, Rabar, Seidler, Cheval, Eckhardt): expect extended multi-week/month drawdowns and flat periods (Abraham 1992 -10.50%, 2005 -10.95%; Parker 2001 -7.98% with only 4 positive months) interleaved with rare large months (Parker Jun-88 +32.42%; Abraham May-88 +32.34%, Jun-88 +71.99%).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not a trade setup; a calibration claim about family-level return distribution.
findings.risk_geometry: None per-trade; the lesson is about portfolio/family-level drawdown tolerance and evaluation horizon.
findings.quote: Their careers are concrete proof of what sticking with a system over the long haul can do for a trading account.
findings.chapter_anchor: Appendix III 'Turtle Performance Data' intro (p.199) and Tables 3.1-3.3 (pp.200-202)
findings.notes: Publishes real monthly return series, the strongest empirical content in this part. Informs V8 lifecycle design: heat caps and screening gates must not terminate a family during its normal losing phase; judge trend families on multi-year frozen-OOS horizons. Expected profile for BTCUSDT 1h trend families is the same right-skew.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

findings.strategy_name: Overconfidence calibration (90% confidence ranges miss ~45% of the time)
findings.mechanism: estimation_calibration: humans systematically overstate the precision of their estimates; trading systems must be built on measured distributions, not self-assessed confidence.
findings.setup_summary: Research practice rule: whenever an edge, parameter, or probability is claimed, require a measured point-in-time distribution; treat self-assessed confidence as systematically overconfident (Eckhardt's 747-weight test: subjects targeting 90%-certain ranges missed 4-5 of 10).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not a trade setup.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated.
findings.quote: Eckhardt said that the majority of people missed about 45 percent of the questions because they were overconfident in their ability to estimate reality.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.13, third Turtle class at Commodities Corporation (pp.183-184)
findings.notes: Supports V8's honest-evidence culture: parameter/edge claims need measured distributions and frozen OOS, not analyst confidence intervals.
findings.book: The Complete Turtle Trader - The Legend, the Lessons, the Results 2007

book_title: Option Spread Strategies: Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets (2009) — Part 2 (Ratio Spreads trade mgmt; Backspreads; Appendix scenarios)

findings.strategy_name: Volatility expansion breakout (backspread as long-vol expression)
findings.mechanism: Low-volatility compression with falling IV is a pre-breakout state; the phase ends with a high-velocity directional move that a long-gamma structure (or, in perp terms, a breakout entry) monetizes.
findings.setup_summary: On BTC 1h: identify a low-volatility consolidation (narrow range, ATR/range contracting over N bars, often with declining volume) between defined support/resistance; if a close occurs beyond the range boundary (the 'breakout/acceleration zone'), enter in the breakout direction with the expectation of a high-magnitude, short-timeframe continuation. Short strike/backstop anchored at the broken S/R level; target zone is the forecast acceleration area.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: close beyond range boundary after sustained compression. Invalidation: no breakout within the forecast horizon (time stop — book: 'if by the close of business Friday the move has not taken place, he should exit'); price re-enters the range (failed breakout); momentum stalls at old S/R.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: breakout bar close (perp analog of long-strike capture); stop: back below the broken boundary (the short strike is 'backstopped by support or resistance'); target: projected acceleration zone; expiry: expiry cycle tied to forecast breakout time, 'buy extra time' (longer expiry) if timing is uncertain; time and price stops both mandatory.
findings.quote: Backspreads, also known as volatility spreads... are used to capture high-magnitude, high-velocity directional moves occurring in a short time frame.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 8 Strategy Overview + Investment Objectives, pp. 223, 238-241
findings.notes: Book frames the trade as buying OTM options financed by an ATM sale; the V8-relevant core is the falsifiable volatility-regime claim (compression precedes expansion) plus the strike rule 'short strike backstopped by support/resistance, long strike in the acceleration zone', which maps to stop placement beyond the compressed range on a perp.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Back-door breakdown acceleration (crowded-long support-break short)
findings.mechanism: After an euphoric, high-volume trend with one-sided (long) crowding, a break of support triggers a crowded exit ('the exit door is going to get awfully small') that accelerates the decline.
findings.setup_summary: On BTC 1h: strong uptrend with rising volume, funding-rate crowding long, and overextension; place a short entry just below each defined support level. Thesis: if support is broken, price accelerates lower rather than drifting; if it holds, no harm (the position is an out-of-the-money 'landmine').
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: close below a support level that was established during the euphoric phase. Invalidation: support holds and close reclaims above it; no acceleration within the forecast window; crowding unwinds without cascade (funding normalizes, no liquidation flush).
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: below support (bar-close or stop-style entry, 'just below each support level'); stop: above the broken support / recent swing; target: accelerated continuation (unbounded in options; perp uses fixed-R or structure target); expiry: short forecast horizon because time decay is the enemy of the long-vol thesis.
findings.quote: If the support lines are broken, the price will accelerate lower, and he places a back door put backspread just below each support level.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 8 Investment Objectives, 'Special Situations' / Back Door Backspreads, pp. 240-241
findings.notes: Crypto-native proxies for the 'everybody is long' condition: funding rate, long/short account ratios, open interest spikes. The cascade is directly testable with perp liquidation data. Requires the participation/flow feature group that is not yet formalized in V8.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Zone-capped deceleration trade (ratio-spread forecast structure)
findings.mechanism: Price decelerates at support/resistance and congestion zones; a slow directional move into a capped target area (with declining vol) is a fading/short-vol opportunity rather than a trend opportunity.
findings.setup_summary: On BTC 1h: slow, grinding directional move into a defined resistance/congestion zone (upside case) or support zone (downside case) with declining realized/implied volatility and weak momentum; fade the move expecting deceleration inside the zone, with the zone as the forecast target anchor.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: grinding approach into the zone with decaying momentum/vol. Invalidation: the boundary is penetrated (the 'lines in the sand' are crossed) or price velocity/magnitude exceeds the forecast, in which case the forecast is wrong and the position must be modified or exited immediately.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: on approach into the zone (limit/close); stop: beyond the zone boundary; target: the opposite side / zone center (option strike math gives max profit at the short strike); expiry: expiration cycle that expires before the projected end of the slow period ('when in doubt, use the expiration cycle that expires before the projected end').
findings.quote: His forecast was for a slow, directional move toward a target area. Hopefully, the target area is capped by a resistance level or a congestion zone above the current underlying price...
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 7 Trade Management, pp. 217-218
findings.notes: The ratio spread itself is short-options (no perp analog), but the underlying forecast discipline — deceleration at S/R with declining vol — is the testable claim. This is a fade-at-zone hypothesis distinct from V8's trend-continuation experts.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Crowding-extreme contrarian (what-if reversal positioning)
findings.mechanism: When participation is overloaded in one direction (overly bullish in an uptrend, overly bearish in a downtrend), the trend is fragile and reversal can be explosive; extremes are a trigger for low-cost contrarian 'what-if' positions.
findings.setup_summary: On BTC 1h/4h: compute a crowding composite (funding rate, long/short ratio, OI growth, media/consensus tone) at trend extremes; when it exceeds a high threshold in the direction of the prevailing trend, stand ready for reversal plays (short after euphoric longs, long after capitulatory shorts) — 'what-if' positions placed like landmines in price zones that would trigger volatility.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: crowding extreme (e.g., funding above high percentile, extreme long/short ratio) concurrent with price at a zone. Invalidation: crowding persists while trend continues (no reversal within horizon); the extreme is followed by more trend, not a snapback.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: limit/close in the trigger zone with bounded risk (the book uses defined-risk backspreads); stop: beyond the trigger zone; target: reversion to the mean/extreme opposite; expiry: short horizon (long-vol thesis decays).
findings.quote: Bullish consensus figures, VIX readings, put/call ratios, media chatter, and so on can be good indicators that market participants are getting either too optimistic or pessimistic.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 8 Investment Objectives, Special Situations, p. 241
findings.notes: Directly transferable: funding rate is a high-frequency, point-in-time crowding measure unique to perps (no VIX/put-call on-chain for BTC in 2009). Proposes a new feature-group input (participation/flow) feeding reversal candidates — complements rather than duplicates the existing 3 active experts.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Dual price+time stop discipline with horizon-matched expiry
findings.mechanism: Time-decay-sensitive positions require a time stop set at setup equal to the forecast horizon, independent of the price stop; if either is hit the thesis is dead.
findings.setup_summary: Every position must be entered with both a price stop and a time stop stated up front; the time stop equals the forecast horizon (e.g., 'breakout this week' — if by the end of the forecast window the move has not occurred, exit). In V8 terms: expiry_bars is a thesis-invalidation (still_valid=false at time expiry), not merely a parameter.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Rule-level: exit on price-stop hit OR time-stop hit (whichever first). The failure mode being prevented is hope-based holding ('tomorrow, definitely tomorrow'), which lets time decay and delta-flip destroy a correct-direction position.
findings.risk_geometry: Expiry_bars set at setup = forecast horizon; if forecast timing is hazy, extend the window deliberately at cost ('buy extra time' with a further expiration) rather than extending silently mid-trade; price stop is separate from time stop.
findings.quote: it is important to have both price and time stop-loss levels. If either is hit, the trader should exit the trade. For example... If by the close of business Friday the move has not taken place, he should exit the trade.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 8 Trade Management, pp. 246
findings.notes: Confirms and sharpens V8's existing expiry_bars lifecycle rule: the book makes time-stop a hard, pre-committed invalidation and explicitly couples it to the forecast horizon. Also gives the 'buy extra time' policy for uncertain timing — a risk_geometry variant, not a mid-trade decision.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Lines-in-the-sand invalidation (boundary breach or velocity overrun kills thesis)
findings.mechanism: Support/resistance boundaries anchored at setup are 'lines in the sand': if the price crosses them, or moves with greater velocity/magnitude than forecast, the forecast is falsified and action is mandatory.
findings.setup_summary: Extends V8's still_valid dead-thesis logic: a thesis is invalidated not only by a level-crossing but also by a velocity/magnitude overrun versus the forecast at setup. Both conditions require immediate modification or exit — 'the investor cannot play mind games with this type of position and must act immediately.'
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: (a) anchor boundary penetrated, or (b) realized bar velocity/magnitude exceeds the forecast band. Consequence: exit or restructure the position without delay.
findings.risk_geometry: Frozen anchor levels (S/R or congestion zones) recorded at setup as risk-management anchors; breach of an anchor or of a velocity bound is an automatic exit trigger; this is distinct from the price stop (which is a fixed loss limit, not a thesis boundary).
findings.quote: If they are penetrated, or if the underlying price begins to move with a greater velocity and in greater magnitudes than the trader had forecast, it is time for him to look for the exit because his forecast is incorrect.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 7 Trade Management, p. 217
findings.notes: Crypto 24/7 amplification: a velocity-overrun invalidation catches liquidation-accelerated moves that a fixed stop at the level alone would miss. Refines V8's existing still_valid semantics rather than proposing a new expert.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Partial-profit scaling with phase-end detection
findings.mechanism: Extract profit progressively as a winning move develops (scaling out / rolling into profits) while keeping residual exposure; exit the residual when the move shows phase-end signals (deceleration, old S/R, vol drop).
findings.setup_summary: Rule for winning positions: scale out a portion at defined milestones as the position moves in favor (book: 'He can slowly scale out of the position as it goes in his favor. This action takes profits and limits remaining risk.'), and treat deceleration / old support-resistance / declining volatility as signals the current phase is ending — exit rather than 'stay too long at the party.'
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger to reduce: profit milestone reached; phase-end signal present. Invalidation of the scaling decision: forecast continues to call for high-magnitude movement — then rolling keeps exposure ('maintaining market exposure') instead of exiting.
findings.risk_geometry: Scale-out fraction and milestone levels defined at setup; remaining risk re-evaluated at each scale point; final exit on phase-end signal or stop, not on hope.
findings.quote: Take Partial Profits... slowly scale out of the position as it goes in his favor. This action takes profits and limits remaining risk.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 7 Trade Management, p. 213; Ch. 8 Trade Management, pp. 244-245
findings.notes: V8's ExposureBook allows partial exits within the one-exposure-per-direction rule; this finding adds the phase-end detection trigger (slowdown at old S/R, vol drop) for the residual exit. Options-specific 'rolling' mechanics are dropped; only the sizing/exit discipline transfers.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Event-risk admission gate (bounded-risk geometry for modest capital)
findings.mechanism: Positions with open-ended adverse risk expose capital to event risk — a large market-moving event can move price so fast that no exit is possible, turning a thesis-error into a catastrophic loss.
findings.setup_summary: RiskGate admission rule: any strategy whose loss is unbounded when a boundary is breached (ratio-spread analog) is gated by an event-risk test — if capital is modest, or overnight/weekend event risk is not tolerable, the trade must be structured with bounded (fixed-R) geometry or declined.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: candidate strategy has open-ended risk on the adverse side. Resolution: either convert to bounded-risk geometry (book: 'The spread can be capped and turned into a limited-risk butterfly') or reject admission.
findings.risk_geometry: Max adverse loss capped at setup; no naked open-ended short exposure; event risk considered continuous (in perp crypto there are no exchange closing gaps, but funding spikes, flash crashes and liquidation cascades are the equivalent event risk on a 24/7 market).
findings.quote: Event risk occurs when a large, market-moving event causes the underlying in which the trader has a ratio spread to gap through her short strikes, leaving no chance to exit the trade or manage risk...
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 7 Trade Management, p. 212
findings.notes: V8 already enforces bounded-risk geometry and one-exposure rules; this finding adds the explicit event-risk admission test and the continuous-risk view (crypto has no gaps but has 24/7 event risk), aligning with V8's risk-percent and heat-cap discipline.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Event pre-pricing / post-event volatility crush
findings.mechanism: Anticipated scheduled events are pre-priced into volatility; once the event resolves, volatility crushes — a position can be right about direction yet lose because the pre-paid premium collapses.
findings.setup_summary: Methodology lesson with a falsifiable perp analog: entering a breakout/momentum position immediately before a scheduled high-impact event (macro releases, liquidations) carries negative expected edge because the move is pre-priced and realized volatility mean-reverts after the event. Test: compare forward returns/vol of entries taken before vs. after scheduled events on BTC.
findings.trigger_invalidation: N/A — methodology lesson, not an executable setup. The scenario: correct 20-point move, long-straddle still only +1 because IV collapsed after the announcement.
findings.risk_geometry: N/A
findings.quote: Even though the movement that was anticipated occurred, the volatility was crushed and the position made very little money.
findings.chapter_anchor: Appendix, Final Exam Part II, Scenario 4, p. 261
findings.notes: No IV surface on perps, but the analog — realized-vol and funding dynamics around scheduled events, and the general point that event positioning is crowded — informs V8's regime filter and event-timing feature work. Presented as practitioner market behavior in a worked exam, no statistics.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Consolidation/continuation breakout in direction of prior trend
findings.mechanism: A consolidation that forms after a trend and breaks out in the direction of that prior trend (continuation pattern) precedes resumption; the breakout itself is the high-velocity event to trade.
findings.setup_summary: On BTC 1h: identify an established trend, then a tight, low-volume consolidation (flag/continuation pattern) against it; a breakout of the consolidation in the direction of the prior trend triggers continuation entry with a target equal to the pre-consolidation range projection.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: close beyond the consolidation boundary in the trend direction. Invalidation: breakout fails and price re-enters the consolidation (failed breakout — reenter the range); no follow-through within the forecast horizon.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: breakout bar close; stop: opposite side of the consolidation (short strike 'backstopped by support or resistance'); target: prior-move extension / acceleration zone; expiry: matched to forecast breakout time.
findings.quote: Consolidation pattern: An area pattern that breaks out in the direction of the previous trend (also called a continuation pattern).
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 8 Concept Review, p. 223; Investment Objectives, pp. 239-240
findings.notes: Corroborates V8's DATA_BLOCKED breakout_retest backlog family (same continuation mechanism; the book adds the continuation-pattern framing and the short-strike-backstop placement rule). Kept DEFER_GATED until a derivatives tape exists, per the existing registry status.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Directionless-market regime filter (sideways suppresses directional experts)
findings.mechanism: When the market is identified as directionless — price decelerating at defined support/resistance with low/declining volatility — the correct posture is limited-risk range/mean-reversion structures; directional trend plays have poor risk-reward.
findings.setup_summary: Regime filter over the active expert set: classify the 1h BTC state as range/directionless when price repeatedly decelerates at S/R zones (boundaries respected) and realized vol is contracting; in that regime, suppress trend-continuation experts (trend_pullback, failed_breakout, liquidity_sweep_reclaim have reduced thesis validity) and let range/mean-reversion candidates (supply_demand_zone) take priority.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Range regime invalidated when a boundary is penetrated (the 'lines in the sand' cross) or a breakout with velocity occurs; regime flips back to trending.
findings.risk_geometry: N/A — regime gating, applied before risk admission; per-expert still_valid conditions remain active within the filter.
findings.quote: Butterflies, condors, and their iron equivalents are limited-risk strategies that can be used during sideways or consolidating markets.
findings.chapter_anchor: Appendix, Final Exam Part II, Scenario 5, p. 262; Ch. 7 Quiz, p. 220
findings.notes: V8 currently has no regime gate (rule 14 keeps shared components ABSENT). This finding proposes the simplest possible form — a per-expert thesis-suppression based on range detection — as a refinement input, not a shared ranker, so it respects the complexity budget.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

findings.strategy_name: Covered call / collar family (synthetic short put)
findings.mechanism: Covered calls and collars are options-market structures (long stock + short call; long put + short call) that synthesize option payoffs (synthetic short put) — they require an options or futures options market that V8's perp-underlying program does not have.
findings.setup_summary: Rejected for V8: no perp-only expression of a covered call or collar exists on a plain BTCUSDT perpetual; the risk-perception lesson ('covered calls are much riskier than perceived — stock is not protected all the way down to zero') is worth keeping only as a general risk-education note, not as an executable family.
findings.trigger_invalidation: N/A
findings.risk_geometry: N/A
findings.quote: Covered calls are much riskier then they are perceived to be because the stock is not protected all the way down to zero, only a portion of it.
findings.chapter_anchor: Appendix, Final Exam Part II, Scenario 1 answers, p. 258; Scenario 3 (collar), p. 261
findings.notes: Honest triage of the options-only chapters that bleed into Part 2's appendix scenarios (covered call, box, collar/reverse-collar). If V8 ever adds an options-data layer, the collar's 'skew makes reverse-collars near-credit' observation would be re-evaluated; today it is REJECT_FOR_V8.
findings.book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

book_title: The Commitments of Traders Bible: How to Profit from Insider Market Intelligence (Briese, 2008)

findings.strategy_name: COT Index commercial extreme setup
findings.mechanism: Hedgers are negative-feedback traders who scale-buy weakness and scale-sell strength; when their normalized net position reaches a historic extreme (percentile of a rolling look-back range), the move that carried them there is exhausted and a reversal setup forms.
findings.setup_summary: Weekly: compute the percentile rank of the commercial (or counterparty) net position within a rolling look-back (book default 36 months, %K-stochastics formula on net positions instead of price). Reading >=90% = commercial buying climax = long setup; <=5% = commercial selling climax = short setup. The extreme alone is not an entry: pair it with a technical breakout-type trigger plus an overriding risk filter (the pattern used by the fund manager Briese profiles, unchanged for 15 years).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: COT Index crosses the 90%/5% threshold; signal is only valid if the trend resumes after it. Invalidation: the extreme fails to produce follow-through - COT buy signals routinely fail in bear markets and sell signals are premature in bull markets, and such failures CONFIRM the prevailing trend rather than reverse it.
findings.risk_geometry: No stop/target stated in the book. Entry is on trend-resumption confirmation, not at the extreme; cited academic work (Wang 2001) found signals profitable out to ~8-week holding periods; commercial extremes are positioned as setups, with the technical trigger supplying the actual entry.
findings.quote: A 90 percent COT reading suggests a commercial buying climax; a 5 percent reading implies an imminent commercial selling climax.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch 6, The COT Index, pp. 63-73; Preface pp. xxi-xxiv
findings.notes: No CFTC-style commercial/speculator segmentation exists for crypto. A funding-rate or OI percentile could proxy the 'positioning extreme', but the smart-money-vs-crowd split is not directly observable, so V8 needs a formalized crypto positioning proxy before this family can be coded.
