findings.setup_summary: Once a position is established with the line of least resistance and confirmed, hold it through normal corrections; exit only when the basic trend visibly changes, not to bank small gains ('you can't go broke taking a profit' is explicitly rejected as a losing philosophy). When margin forces a reduction, close the losing position first and keep the winning one. Big money comes from the big swings; small point-clipping only served to build the original stake.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Exit signal is a change in the line of least resistance / basic trend reversal, not an adverse wiggle and not a profit target; the thesis must visibly break.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: as the probe/pyramid method; stop: 10% cap; target: open-ended ride of the swing (no fixed R-multiple); expiry: none - position ends on trend change.
findings.quote: The big money was in the big swings, in waiting for the basic trend to play out and riding the stock for as long as possible... Always sell the loser, keep the winner; he knew the rule, but he did not act on it.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 4 'The Crash of 1907' (p. 66); Ch. 5 'The Cotton King' (p. 93)
findings.notes: Directly relevant to V8's trend_pullback family: target_r 1.0 + expiry 8 bars may be too small to capture 'the big swing'; suggests thesis-based (still_valid) exits over fixed small R-targets, and a lifecycle rule that winners are never cut to fund losers. Any change must challenge the frozen OOS baseline first (registry discipline).
findings.book: Jesse Livermore - World's Greatest Stock Trader 2001

findings.strategy_name: News-reaction asymmetry (bad news discounts slowly in a bull regime)
findings.mechanism: identical news moves price differently by regime; in an uptrend negative news is initially absorbed and prices rebound, so the tradable turn appears only when price action confirms the regime change, not on the news itself
findings.setup_summary: After a major negative exogenous event (e.g., the 1906 San Francisco earthquake) during an established uptrend, expect the initial shock to be absorbed and prices to rebound to former levels (Livermore went flat, made nothing on the initial move). The short thesis becomes actionable only when the market thereafter fails to advance - rallies falter and stocks slide back from old highs - then short/add into the failing rally. Trade the price reaction to the event, never the event itself.
findings.trigger_invalidation: If after the event price keeps making new highs and holds, the reaction thesis is invalidated; a violent one-day shock drop alone is not the signal (Livermore was 'flat on the trade' after the initial shock move).
findings.risk_geometry: Entry: short on failed rally / break of the prior low after the event (bar-close basis); stop: 10% cap; target: ride the new downtrend; no fixed expiry.
findings.quote: Livermore knew that bad news in a bull market climate takes a lot longer to sink in with the public than bad news in a bear market, when the climate is already negative.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 3 'The San Francisco Earthquake Rumbles in New York' (pp. 59-60); the confirmation principle it implements is 'To anticipate the market is to gamble; to be patient and react only when the market gives the signal is to speculate' (p. 54)
findings.notes: Single anecdote, so NARRATIVE evidence, not a candidate for an active expert. In 24/7 perp crypto with high leverage and near-instant information flow, news is discounted faster, weakening the 'slow sink-in' asymmetry; still, regime-dependent reaction to exogenous events is a testable feature input for the response feature group (e.g., post-shock rally-failure detection as a location/response feature).
findings.book: Jesse Livermore - World's Greatest Stock Trader 2001

book_title: Jesse Livermore: World's Greatest Stock Trader (Richard Smitten, 2001)
The Broker (John Grisham, 2005)

findings.strategy_name: Relative-value convergence arbitrage (snap trade / spread reversion)
findings.mechanism: Historically stable relative spreads between two economically linked instruments (futures-vs-bills, on-the-run-vs-off-the-run Treasurys, Italy-vs-swaps) widen to an extreme and then converge; profit comes from the spread normalizing regardless of absolute market direction.
findings.setup_summary: Two linked instruments whose historical spread has widened far beyond its normal range, where a concrete convergence mechanism exists (same issuer, maturity link, or arbitrage relationship). Buy the cheap leg, short the dear leg; position is direction-neutral. Entry on the extreme-widening signal; exit on partial/full normalization or a time bound. LTCM's concrete version: the off-the-run 30y Treasury yielding 12bp more than the on-the-run; $1B long cheap / $1B short dear, held a few months until the spread 'snapped'.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Thesis dies when the convergence mechanism is structurally broken (credit regime change, issuer stress, shift in who holds the paper). Spread widening beyond the entry thesis's stress bound invalidates the holding premise, not just the entry.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry at market on the spread extreme; no conventional stop since the position is held for convergence; real risk is the adverse excursion (spread can go 12bp to 14bp to 20bp) against leverage and margin; expiry is the convergence horizon (months, e.g., the snap trade 'snapped after only a few months'); target is spread normalization, and LTCM 'preferred to reap a sure nickel than to gamble on an uncertain dollar' via ~25x leverage.
findings.quote: the two bonds usually snapped together after only a few months
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.3 'On the Run', pp.43-45 (also Ch.1 Eckstein futures-vs-bills pp.3-5; Ch.3 Italy-vs-swaps pp.56-59)
findings.notes: LTCM's edge was financing (zero haircut repo) and experience reading models, not unique models ('other Wall Street firms had also found their way to MIT'). No on-the-run/off-the-run analog exists inside a single BTCUSDT perp, so this is data-blocked in V8: it needs a second instrument (perp-vs-spot basis, cross-venue spread, funding-based carry) and the cross_market feature group, which V8 does not yet ingest. The 1998 failure of this exact family is captured in finding 3.
findings.book: When Genius Failed - The Rise and Fall of Long-Term Capital Management 2001

findings.strategy_name: Fat-tailed returns and non-stationary volatility (critique of 'risk = historical volatility')
findings.mechanism: Black-Scholes treated volatility as a constant, inherent trait and Merton assumed continuous time (no jumps); in reality returns are leptokurtic and markets gap, so any sizing, stop, or loss-odds estimate built from historical volatility systematically underprices tail losses.
findings.setup_summary: Methodological constraint, not a trade setup: Fama's documented finding is that for individual stocks, a price move of more than 5 standard deviations should occur once per ~7,000 years under a normal distribution but in fact occurs about once every 3-4 years. Any V8 expert or RiskGate that converts realized/historical volatility into position size, stop distance (atr_stop), expiry, or 'loss odds' must be audited for fat tails; Black Monday (a 23% single-day drop, ~1-in-a-trillion under normality) is the canonical counterexample.
findings.trigger_invalidation: n/a - the finding is that a 5+ sigma 1h-bar move is always in the near tail; a vol-derived sizing rule is invalidated whenever it assumes log-normality. Also 'markets have memories' (momentum/herding), so the i.i.d. random-walk premise fails.
findings.risk_geometry: stop_distance_atr, expiry_bars, and leverage set from realized vol inherit the fat-tail error; tail-aware alternatives are robust quantiles of realized excursions rather than sigma multiples; LTCM's own disclosure ('lose at least 5% in 1 month in 5, 10%+ in 1 in 10, 20%+ only 1 year in 50') is precisely the miscalibration this finding warns about.
findings.quote: more than five standard deviations from the mean should be observed about once every 7,000 years. In fact such observations seem to occur about once every three to four years.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.4 'Dear Investors', pp.61-74 (Fama's fat-tail thesis pp.70-72; Black Monday pp.68, 72-73)
findings.notes: Crypto perps are more volatile and more leptokurtic than 1994 bond markets, and 24/7 trading with no price limits/auction halt means gap/overshoot risk materializes intra-bar. Also the book's volatility-targeting description (LTCM borrowed more when portfolio 'too quiet', reduced leverage when 'too volatile') shows vol-targeting was itself a mechanism, not just an estimate - but it rests on the same fragile vol estimate.
findings.book: When Genius Failed - The Rise and Fall of Long-Term Capital Management 2001

findings.strategy_name: Leverage-forced-selling cascade and stress correlation collapse
findings.mechanism: Leverage converts a loss into forced selling; when many leveraged players hold nominally diversified positions, the common forced-sell channel makes every asset/spread fall together, so diversification is illusory in stress ('You don't sell what you should. You sell what you can.').
findings.setup_summary: Standing risk rule: cap aggregate exposure whose exit requires buying/selling into a stressed market, because in a forced-sell regime every leg unwinds simultaneously - LTCM was 'buying the stuff that everyone wanted to sell' in every market, so its assets 'would be susceptible to falling in unison if a time came when literally everyone wanted to sell.' A per-instrument/direction exposure cap is insufficient; assumed correlation across strategies/venues must spike toward 1 under funding spikes or liquidation cascades.
findings.trigger_invalidation: n/a - this is a standing cap. The correct reaction to a stress signal (funding spike, liquidation volume, spread blow-out) is to reduce, not to add.
findings.risk_geometry: Heat cap / correlated exposure cap; any liquidity-provision-style trade must carry an explicit exit plan because liquidity 'is a straw man' - there is no liquidity for the community as a whole, and if you are not in debt you cannot be made to sell.
findings.quote: You don't sell what you should. You sell what you can.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.3 'On the Run', pp.41-43; Rosenfeld liquidity-provision admission pp.44-45
findings.notes: The 1994 rout (Steinhardt losing $800M in four days, Soros $650M in two) and LTCM's 1998 collapse are the book's core evidence that spread trades that are 'balanced enough to be safe' all break together when the same leveraged owners are forced to sell - direct support for V8's correlated exposure cap and for treating diversification claims with suspicion.
findings.book: When Genius Failed - The Rise and Fall of Long-Term Capital Management 2001

findings.strategy_name: Survival gap for reversion/convergence trades (patient capital vs time-to-convergence)
findings.mechanism: A trade that is 'right' on thesis can still ruin the trader: the adverse excursion can exceed the capital available before the expected reversion arrives. Survival depends on duration-matched capital and funding, not on thesis correctness.
findings.setup_summary: For any mean-reversion expert (pullback_in_trend, band reversion, spread reversion), the time-to-reversion has a wide right tail; episode risk_geometry must set expiry_bars bounded by capital-at-risk and funding durability, not by the thesis. LTCM's design answer - a 3-year investor lockup so it could 'be the bank that could tell depositors, Come back tomorrow' - bought patience, but the August-September 1998 excursion overwhelmed even that capital, so the lockup did not remove the gap.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Thesis-invalidation (still_valid) and capital survival are separate exits: a position can be thesized right and still must be cut when loss exceeds what the book can bear. 'Spreads eventually always came in' was the lesson Meriwether 'could count on' - and the equally valuable lesson he missed until 1998.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry at bar close on the extreme; no tight stop while thesis is intact, but a hard capital-based cut plus an expiry measured in the instrument's convergence horizon; target = normalization. In V8 this means frozen refs + a funded patience budget, not an open-ended hold.
findings.quote: a losing trade may well turn around eventually... but the turn could arrive too late to do the trader any good--meaning, of course, that he might go broke in the interim.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.1 'Meriwether', pp.9-10 (Eckstein-affair lesson); lockup design Ch.2 'Hedge Fund', p.27
findings.notes: In crypto perps, funding and vol mean-revert quickly but adverse excursions (liquidation cascades) can exceed a naive expiry; this bounds how long a reversion expert may hold and justifies V8's explicit expiry_bars plus capital-based risk gate rather than thesis-only expiry.
findings.book: When Genius Failed - The Rise and Fall of Long-Term Capital Management 2001

findings.strategy_name: Model-conviction doubling (adding size to a losing position)
findings.mechanism: Conviction in the model converts a losing trade into a signal to add size ('merely redoubled the bet'); at leverage this turns a paper loss into a potentially catastrophic loss, and when traders are their own watchdogs there is no independent brake.
findings.setup_summary: RiskGate rule: prohibit or strictly cap scaling into a position that is moving against the entry thesis purely because model conviction is unchanged; any size addition must be justified by a new, independently observable condition, not by conviction. Canonical case: Hilibrand lost $400M on a Salomon mortgage bet and coolly proposed doubling the commitment; management refused the doubling and the position eventually recovered, but the pattern is the risk.
findings.trigger_invalidation: n/a - the rule holds regardless of thesis; conviction is not a valid re-entry signal.
findings.risk_geometry: Fixed per-episode size; no pyramiding into losers; admission must flow through a deterministic RiskGate because 'the traders were their own watchdogs' is the failure mode - LTCM had no Gutfreund-type brake and no independent risk manager, and risk approvals went to Hilibrand/Haghani 'who would fight relentlessly for what they wanted.'
findings.quote: If a trade went against them, the arbitrageurs, especially the ever-confident Hilibrand, merely redoubled the bet.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch.1 'Meriwether', p.13; Hilibrand mortgage loss and self-monitoring critique Ch.3 'On the Run', pp.58-59
findings.notes: Perp leverage plus 1h-bar moves makes averaging into a loser especially dangerous because a liquidation threshold converts the intended add into a forced stop-out; this supports V8's deterministic RiskGate admission and its ban on in-place learning/parameter mutation mid-episode.
findings.book: When Genius Failed - The Rise and Fall of Long-Term Capital Management 2001

book_title: When Genius Failed: The Rise and Fall of Long-Term Capital Management (2001) - Roger Lowenstein
The New New Thing - A Silicon Valley Story (Michael Lewis)

findings.strategy_name: Herd head-fake (consensus theme displacement)
findings.mechanism: When capital consensus herds into one technology theme while a dismissed alternative quietly scales, the herd position is the fragile one and the displaced alternative wins the repricing.
findings.setup_summary: Lesson-level, not a tradable setup. In 1992-94 the world's largest media/software companies and their investors all herded into building the interactive-TV 'telecomputer' (SGI/Time Warner Orlando ITV, AT&T, Microsoft, Oracle); the actual winner was the ignored Internet (Netscape), which within six months made the entire herd look wrong. Crypto-perp analogue would be: extreme crowding into one narrative sector while an adjacent ignored narrative accrues volume/flow is a fragility signal, not a confirmation signal.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Invalidated if consensus-crowded themes systematically outperform displaced alternatives in follow-on repricings.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated; the book describes an allocation-level event, not an entry/stop/target structure.
findings.quote: Then, just as they all ran as a herd in one direction, he took off in another. And within six months he made them all look like fools. It was one of the great unintentional head fakes in the history of technology.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'Inventing Jim Clark'
findings.notes: n=1 event in equity capital allocation; no price-level mechanism stated, so it cannot be formalized as an expert today. At most a qualitative warning: consensus crowding as anti-confirmation for narrative trades (funding/long-bias extremes).
findings.book: The New New Thing - A Silicon Valley Story 2014

findings.strategy_name: Rule-of-thumb regime flip (market acceptance thresholds are mutable)
findings.mechanism: A single celebrated success can suspend a long-standing market acceptance rule, repricing the whole asset class on a new criterion while the prior regime's incumbents decay.
findings.setup_summary: Equity-IPO market: pre-1995 rule of thumb required four consecutive profitable quarters before selling a tech company to the public; Netscape's loss-making August 1995 IPO established 'rapid growth, not profits' as the new acceptance criterion. Incumbent SGI, peaking at $44 the week after the offering, fell steadily to $8 over the following four years and its CEO was fired. Lesson for V8: the market's acceptance/valuation threshold is itself a regime variable, not a constant - a static 'still_valid' rule tied to a stale threshold can break.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Invalidated if a market that suspends an acceptance rule fails to reprice incumbents (i.e., if no repricing follows the threshold flip).
findings.risk_geometry: None stated (equity-IPO structure, not a trade).
findings.quote: it had long been a rule of thumb with the Silicon Valley venture capitalists that they didn't peddle a new technology company to the investing public until it had had at least four consecutive profitable quarters. Netscape had nothing to show investors but massive losses. But its fabulous stock market success created a precedent. No longer did you need to show profits; you needed to show rapid growth.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'Inventing Jim Clark'
findings.notes: Market-structure fact described in narrative; no statistical backtest. Supports designing regime filters with time-varying thresholds rather than hard-coded acceptance rules. Not formalizable as a perp price expert from this text alone.
findings.book: The New New Thing - A Silicon Valley Story 2014

findings.strategy_name: Edge decay and forced self-cannibalization
findings.mechanism: A working edge is systematically self-limiting: the constituency earning from the current product resists the change that would replace it, while the underlying force (Moore's law) commoditizes the edge from below - so the incumbent that defends the present over the future loses.
findings.setup_summary: Clark's explicit rule: a technology company 'needed always to be looking to destroy itself. If it didn't, someone else would.' SGI refused to build the sub-$5,000 low-end machine that would cannibalize its high-margin workstations and was displaced by the PC/Microsoft. Direct V8 lesson: a currently-profitable strategy variant's constituency resists replacement, so challenger evaluation must be institutionalized and forced (V8's frozen-OOS challenger + registry protocol does this); the currently-best variant is the most likely to be over-trusted.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Invalidated if incumbents that defend the current product systematically outperform self-cannibalizers over horizons the thesis cares about.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated.
findings.quote: For a technology company to succeed, he argued, it needed always to be looking to destroy itself. If it didn't, someone else would. 'It's the hardest thing in business to do,' he would say.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 4 'Disorganization Man'
findings.notes: Practitioner heuristic. 24/7, no-barrier perp markets accelerate edge commoditization/crowding, so the lesson maps most strongly onto V8's own challenger/registry evolution and the ban on in-place version mutation (rule 15).
findings.book: The New New Thing - A Silicon Valley Story 2014

findings.strategy_name: Premature entry as failure mode (correct thesis, wrong timing)
findings.mechanism: A directionally correct thesis entered before the enabling condition (cost/infrastructure/readiness) matures burns capital; the loss comes from timing, not thesis validity.
findings.setup_summary: Clark's telecomputer thesis was directionally correct (interactive home computing) but entered years early at unbuildable cost: 'too expensive to build' and 25M Internet users later, the same idea grafted onto the Internet succeeded. Trading analogue: a setup with correct direction but entered before the confirmation/cost-feasibility condition is met still loses; entry timing and build-cost constraints are as binding as thesis validity. Supports V8's separation of thesis validity from entry gating and time-based expiry discipline.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Invalidated if being early with a correct thesis is systematically profitable rather than capital-destructive.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry timing and feasibility (cost) act as the binding gate; the book states no stop/target/expiry numbers.
findings.quote: He was wrong about all of this, at least in his timing. He was off and running down a dark tunnel that ran directly into a brick wall. But at least he was running. ... 'Now he said that his telecomputer was ahead of its time. It was too expensive to build.'
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'Inventing Jim Clark' (Siggraph telecomputer talk; kitchen-table pivot to the Internet)
findings.notes: Narrative illustration, not a statistical case. Read for V8 as a lifecycle lesson: expiry/time-gating exists to stop correct-thesis-early entries from bleeding; thesis can be right while the entry is wrong.
findings.book: The New New Thing - A Silicon Valley Story 2014

findings.strategy_name: Complexity-adoption bias (intellectual elegance vs payoff)
findings.mechanism: The more intellectually appealing a mechanism, the less likely the market will pay for it - engineering elegance/aggressiveness is a negative adoption signal, not a positive one.
findings.setup_summary: Explicit practitioner rule drawn from the Orlando ITV project - 'the most aggressive supercomputer project ever put together in the history of the world,' costing $5,000 per black box - which nobody bought: the appeal of a product to its builders is inversely related to willingness to pay ('A thousand people don't build anything; if you need to build something really complicated really fast, you hire fifty of the smartest people you can find'). V8 lesson: favor simple, low-dimensional, falsifiable hypotheses over maximally sophisticated ones; complexity is a false-precision risk, consistent with rule 14's complexity budget.
findings.trigger_invalidation: n/a (heuristic, not an empirical claim).
findings.risk_geometry: None stated.
findings.quote: It's a good rule of the technology business that the more intellectually appealing a machine, the less likely anyone will pay for it.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'Inventing Jim Clark' (Orlando ITV project)
findings.notes: Stated explicitly as a rule. For V8 this is a research-program guard: an expert whose mechanism is beautiful/complex is more likely to be over-fit and under-adopted; the program should weight evidence from simple mechanisms first. No feature-group mapping.
findings.book: The New New Thing - A Silicon Valley Story 2014

book_title: University of Berkshire Hathaway: 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting (Part 2: 2009-2015 + appendices)

findings.strategy_name: Survival-first ruin-avoidance (play tomorrow)
findings.setup_summary: Portfolio-level rule for BTCUSDT 1h replay: the book must never be placed in a state where a realistic adverse sequence (repeated stop-outs, or a fat-tail bar at maximum allowed leverage) can wipe the account. Concretely: a hard max-drawdown cap, a per-episode leverage cap, and a standing reserve of uncommitted exposure; admission of any episode is refused if (current drawdown + worst-case episode loss) would breach the cap.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: sizing/admission check at candidate-entry time. Dead state: if realized drawdown reaches the cap, all exposure is flattened and entry gated until the cap resets.
findings.risk_geometry: No bar-level entry/stop/target stated in book; stated analogs are 'keep plenty in reserves', 'go low on debt', and a fixed minimum cash cushion ($20B at Berkshire).
findings.quote: Buffett noted that his first rule is to play tomorrow. That means not going broke no matter what happens.
findings.chapter_anchor: 2012 annual meeting, 'Systemic Risk' discussion
findings.notes: Direct port to RiskGate: max-drawdown cap + leverage cap + reserve. The existing one-exposure-per-direction and heat cap already approximate the reserve discipline. Framed as survival-first, not edge.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Panic-liquidity provision (be greedy when others are fearful)
findings.setup_summary: On BTCUSDT 1h, long after a panic signature: forced-deleveraging flush (deeply negative funding, open-interest contraction via liquidations, capitulation-sized down bars) - the moment when 'naked swimmers call Berkshire'. Entry next-bar close; thesis is that loss-aversion sellers have overpaid to exit and the flush is exhausted; exit on structure reclaim or expiry.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: panic state (extreme negative funding + liquidation cascade + climax down-bar). Invalidation: price keeps making new lows with expanding participation/volume - the flush is regime change, not exhaustion.
findings.risk_geometry: Book states no explicit entry/stop/target; only the discipline of fast decisive action in panics ('the time for that transaction was NOW'). For V8: entry next-bar close, stop beyond panic low or ATR multiple, expiry in bars, capped heat.
findings.quote: Berkshire is the 800 number when there is a panic in the markets
findings.chapter_anchor: 2013 annual meeting, '1-800-BRK-Deal'; 2011 'Fear and Opportunity'
findings.notes: Corroborates the existing backlog family 'capitulation' (mechanism capitulation_exhaustion) and adds the premium-harvest framing: the counterparty to loss-aversion exits gets paid. Crypto perps lack a fundamental 'value' anchor, so 'cheap' must be proxied by flow/liquidation data, not intrinsic value.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Fat-tail aware risk modeling (Gaussian underestimates)
findings.setup_summary: Modeling rule for the simulator and RiskGate: do not size, price, or stress-test with normal-distribution assumptions (VaR explicitly derided by Munger); calibrate stop/entry costs and stress scenarios from the realized fat-tailed distribution of BTCUSDT bar ranges and cascade episodes.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Standing model rule: any stress scenario or stop-cost estimate derived from Gaussian/VaR methods is rejected; stress tests must include realized fat-tail events.
findings.risk_geometry: Not stated in book; transferable claim is that loss-distribution tails must be modeled from empirical extremes, which directly sets stop distance and sizing.
findings.quote: Risk on Wall Street may be measured with Gaussian curves, but the fat tails are not fat enough!
findings.chapter_anchor: 2012 annual meeting, 'Remembering What Can Go Wrong' (Munger on VaR: 'one of the dumbest ideas ever put forward')
findings.notes: Lands in simulator stress scenarios plus RiskGate sizing; supports the deleveraging-cascade tail already implied by liquidity_vacuum_reentry.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Anti-herding abstention (refuse inadequate pricing)
findings.setup_summary: Admission discipline: the system must not add or hold exposure merely because participation is high or because the strategy is 'obviously working' for others (bandwagon/social-proof effect, envy of the neighbor). Concretely: abstention is an explicit output - when a setup's pricing is inadequate (funding already rich, edge crowded), the correct action is no trade, like Berkshire walking away from insurance when prices are wrong.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: candidate episode offered at inadequate pricing (crowded participation / rich premium). Invalidation: if crowding metrics keep rising without a thesis re-set, do not chase; the dead-thesis discipline applies symmetrically to the urge to participate.
findings.risk_geometry: No entry/stop/target; the rule is refusal/abstention.
findings.quote: you can't afford to go along with the crowd in investment or insurance or a lot of things.
findings.chapter_anchor: 2013 annual meeting, 'Reinsurance Primer' ('We haven't left the market. The market left us.'); 2012 'Avoiding Mistakes'
findings.notes: Supports RiskGate deterministic admission and the absence of FOMO-driven variants; the mirror of the dead-thesis (still_valid) exit.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Circle-of-competence filter (restricted state space)
findings.setup_summary: Pre-screening methodology: restrict the trading universe and state space to what can be characterized over a meaningful horizon (BTCUSDT 1h only, one behavior family per expert); candidates that cannot be characterized are filtered out before screening effort is spent ('use filters so you don't waste time on unproductive ideas').
findings.trigger_invalidation: Standing methodology; not a tradeable setup.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated.
findings.quote: Know and stay within your circle of competence.
findings.chapter_anchor: 2012 annual meeting, 'Avoiding Mistakes'; 2014 'Filters'
findings.notes: Rationalizes one-expert-per-behavior-family and the frozen feature-group spec; argues against scope creep into uncharacterized instruments or timeframes.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Risk-selection segmentation (underwrite each state differently)
findings.setup_summary: Segmentation lesson from insurance underwriting: pooling all market states and estimating one parameter set 'treats 16-year-olds like 82-year-olds'; stratify the BTCUSDT 1h sample by risk-defining features (volatility regime, participation, time) and estimate per-segment thresholds; a variant is only credible with large, credible per-segment samples.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Standing methodology: a pooled-sample estimate that ignores segmentation is not admissible as evidence.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated in book.
findings.quote: if your risk-selection process treats 16 year olds like 82 year olds, you're going to get horrible underwriting results.
findings.chapter_anchor: 2013 annual meeting, 'Auto Insurance Primer' ('data must be credible and reliable. Large amounts of data are required to achieve this.')
findings.notes: Justifies condition-specific variants of a family and the large-sample screening evidence bar (parameter changes = variants of one family).
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Evidence-gated iteration (repeat what works)
findings.setup_summary: Iteration discipline: every new challenger/variant must beat the currently-formalized baseline on frozen OOS before promotion - the opportunity-cost framing ('each extra dollar should go where it gets the best risk-adjusted return'); keep what works, drop what doesn't, and mine documented failures (financial follies) as literature input.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Standing methodology: a challenger that does not beat baseline on frozen OOS is not promoted.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated.
findings.quote: That's the fundamental algorithm of life—REPEAT WHAT WORKS.
findings.chapter_anchor: 2010 annual meeting, 'Pragmatism'; 2015 'Culture' ('always dissatisfied with what we already knew')
findings.notes: Mirrors V8's registry experiment protocol (challenger + frozen OOS + registry decision) and the opportunity-cost calibration of which ideas deserve capital.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Avoid newly-listed instruments (insider timing)
findings.setup_summary: Lifecycle rule: do not trade perp instruments with insufficient listing history - the party that creates/lists the instrument chooses the timing, so early history carries adverse-selection and supply-overhang risk ('the insiders are selling their company'). Concretely: a perp is eligible only after a minimum bar history supports a credible sample and liquidity.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: candidate on an instrument younger than the minimum listing age. Invalidation: instrument becomes eligible when history/liquidity thresholds are met.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated in book.
findings.quote: Avoid new issues—the insiders are selling their company, so it's ridiculous to think that an IPO will be the cheapest thing to buy in a world of thousands of stocks.
findings.chapter_anchor: 2012 annual meeting, 'Avoiding Mistakes'
findings.notes: Applies if the V8 universe expands beyond BTCUSDT to alt perps; trivially satisfied for BTC itself. Maps to a listing-age gate in lifecycle.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Monetary-regime valuation anchor (interest rates as gravity)
findings.setup_summary: Regime filter: broad rate/liquidity conditions are the gravity that sets the level of all asset prices - near-zero rates and liquidity pumping buoy risk assets regardless of micro structure, and the market reprices when the regime turns (the impact lands 'when the market senses the Fed has changed course'). For BTCUSDT: gate long-bias risk on a cross_market monetary-regime feature (rates, DXY, liquidity) rather than treating each 1h setup in isolation.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Trigger: candidate episodes assessed against the prevailing monetary-regime feature. Invalidation: regime flip (rates rising / liquidity turning) downgrades long setups and upgrades repricing risk.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated (macro-level claim).
findings.quote: Interest rates are to asset prices sort of like gravity is to the apple.
findings.chapter_anchor: 2013 annual meeting, 'Effects of ZBIR'; 2015 'Stock Market and Interest Rates' (market cap to GDP at 125%, corporate profits to GDP >10%)
findings.notes: Needs cross_market data (rates/DXY/liquidity) that the current frozen spec does not carry; the total-marketcap-to-GDP / profit-share screens are the BTC MVRV-analog valuation check. DEFER_GATED until data exists.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Beauty-contest pricing of non-producing assets
findings.setup_summary: Structural framing: BTC produces nothing, so its price is set by the Keynesian beauty contest - what matters is what others believe others believe ('rising prices create their own excitement... the neighbor gets rich'). Consequence for BTCUSDT 1h: herding/trend persistence is a first-order dynamic that can run far beyond any 'fair' value, and fundamental-value anchors are unavailable; both momentum persistence and crowd-following risk are amplified.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Standing framing; implies trend/momentum families should expect long persistence tails, and 'value'-anchored mean-reversion should not assume a fair-value magnet.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated.
findings.quote: you are betting not on whom you believe to be the prettiest contestant, but who others will believe is beautiful
findings.chapter_anchor: 2012 annual meeting, 'The Three Categories of Investment' (Keynes, General Theory ch. 12)
findings.notes: Supports the expectation that herding persistence dominates BTCUSDT and cautions the capitulation backlog against any intrinsic-value anchoring.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Worst-case underwriting (reserve conservatively)
findings.setup_summary: Per-episode sizing rule: price every position as if the worst case will occur - set risk_geometry (stop distance, atr_ref, size) from the conservative end of the realized distribution so the worst-case adverse path stays survivable; keep a standing reserve so a single episode or a cluster of episodes cannot threaten the book.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Standing sizing rule: a sizing that assumes the average case instead of the worst case is not admissible.
findings.risk_geometry: Book states only the principle ('assume the worst and price from there') and a $20B minimum cash cushion; no bar-level parameters.
findings.quote: Buffett's tactic is to assume the worst and price from there.
findings.chapter_anchor: 2012 annual meeting, 'Insurance' discussion (reserving conservatively; 'It's inevitable that some contracts work out worse than expected.')
findings.notes: Distinct from the portfolio-level max_drawdown_cap: this is the per-episode sizing layer feeding risk_geometry and the stop/atr_ref spec.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Observation-cadence discipline (no daily quotations)
findings.setup_summary: Discipline on how often the system looks at the tape: higher observation frequency degrades decisions - 'most people would invest better with no daily quotations'; marginal, low-conviction signals should be dropped rather than traded. For BTCUSDT 1h: respect expiry_bars and thesis horizons; do not let every intermediate bar alter a live thesis (separate noise exits from dead-thesis exits).
findings.trigger_invalidation: Standing discipline: trade only signals above a conviction/quality threshold; premature noise exits are treated as a process error.
findings.risk_geometry: None stated; relates to expiry_bars and the still_valid/dead-thesis distinction.
findings.quote: most people would invest better with no daily quotations. Buy a good business, and hold it for a long, long time.
findings.chapter_anchor: 2011 annual meeting, 'Fear and Opportunity'; 2013 'Energy Management' (decision fatigue: 'you shouldn't make important decisions when you're tired')
findings.notes: Transferable to V8 as signal selectivity plus expiry discipline; the fatigue point is human-specific but the 'fewer, higher-quality signals' corollary is machine-relevant.
findings.book: University of Berkshire Hathaway - 30 Years of Lessons Learned from Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger at the Annual Shareholders Meeting 2017

findings.strategy_name: Counter-trend pullback against a 50-day MA trend (with trend-side hedge)
findings.mechanism: Trends lumber in fits and spurts while counter-trends are swift, brief retracements that lose momentum and revert to the trend
findings.setup_summary: Define trend by the 50-day moving average (close below 50MA = bearish, above = bullish). In an established trend, trade counter-trend pullbacks actively with liberal stops, while a trend-side position (book: an option) accumulates value along the trend; exit the counter-trend leg the moment its momentum fades.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Crossing the 50-day MA invalidates the trend call; if a pullback extends past a brief retracement it is a fundamental shift into new trend territory, not a counter-trend.
findings.risk_geometry: Entry on pullback within trend; stops used liberally to exit counter-trend legs; trend-side hedge held through; counter-trends in the book's gold chart lasted at most ~8 days (expiry-like duration).
findings.quote: Counter-trends typically behave differently. They are swift and aggressive and are actually the retracement opportunities that develop from the actual trend. There is fast money to make and lose during counter-trends.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 Precision Trading at Its Finest pp. 92-101; trend/counter-trend pp. 60-61
findings.notes: Refinement input for src/v8/experts/trend_pullback.py: add 50-period MA trend filter and note counter-trend brevity when setting expiry_bars. Book's scheme is both-direction (fade counter-trend); V8's formalized family is LONG-only, so the counter-trend variant is a variant proposal, not a new family.
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Fixed-percentage per-trade risk cap and drawdown-aware loss control
findings.mechanism: Leveraged loss recovery is nonlinear (a 10% loss needs 11% back; 50% at 5:1 needs 200%), so capping per-trade loss and monitoring max drawdown preserves capital for the few big winners
findings.setup_summary: Cap risk per trade at a fixed percentage of account value (book cites CTA standard of no more than 2% per trade); compute drawdown and maximum drawdown as program-level limits; model the leverage-scaled recovery requirement after any loss.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not a setup strategy; program-level invariant.
findings.risk_geometry: Per-trade risk cap ~2% (CTA standard; retail often 5-10%); maximum-drawdown halt levels; halve effective leverage by doubling committed capital.
findings.quote: CTAs typically attempt to control their loss at a fixed percentage of no more than 2 percent on any given trade.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 1 pp. 18-20 (also leverage math p. 18, Rockwell/Hieronymous/Barber-Odean studies pp. 19-20)
findings.notes: Feeds src/v8/risk.py RiskGate: per-trade risk fraction, drawdown/max-drawdown and heat caps. Recovery arithmetic is falsifiable; Hieronymous (92% of one-time traders lose), Rockwell Study (18 yrs), and Barber & Odean 2004 are cited statistics.
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Event straddle/strangle: both-sides positioning into scheduled announcements
findings.mechanism: Scheduled high-impact announcements compress range beforehand and force a directional expansion afterward; buying both sides monetizes the expansion without predicting direction
findings.setup_summary: When a market has been moving sideways and a scheduled high-impact event (rate decision, CPI, jobless claims, PPI) approaches, enter both sides simultaneously (buy straddle at-the-money or cheaper OTM strangle); once direction resolves, cut the losing leg immediately and ride the winner, optionally converting the winner to a longer position.
findings.trigger_invalidation: If price never expands (announcement in line, market stays flat), time decay erodes both legs - theta loss is the thesis-invalidator.
findings.risk_geometry: Max loss = initial premium outlay; cut losing leg as soon as direction resolves; strangle preferred when at-the-money vol is rich (book: strangle risked ~1 to gain ~2 on the 397-tick gold example); slippage risk on fast exit.
findings.quote: Instead of forcing an artificial or rumored direction on your trading, use a straddle to establish your initial position.
findings.notes: The straddle vehicle needs an options market V8 does not have (perp-only linear), so the family is DEFER_GATED/backlog. Transferable pieces: pre-event range-compression detection and an event-calendar time feature as FEATURE_INPUT candidates; crypto reacts to CPI/FOMC/ETF decisions with similar expansion but fewer scheduled movers.
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Consensus-exhausted announcement reversal (sell-the-news / market-not-following-news)
findings.mechanism: When analysts have talked up a consensus outcome and the market has already moved in that direction before the announcement, post-announcement follow-through fails and profit-taking reverses price
findings.setup_summary: Before a scheduled announcement, if expectations are widely known, analysts have talked up figures excessively, and price has already run in the expected direction, fade the post-announcement continuation: anticipate a quick selloff/bounce against the consensus. Book's crude-oil inventory case: bearish inventory news dropped price one day, then price broke out to new highs.
findings.trigger_invalidation: If the actual number surprises beyond consensus, momentum continues with the news and the reversal thesis fails.
findings.risk_geometry: Reversal entry after the event print; stop beyond the pre-event range; book example target was a large extension (~$11/bbl over ~2 weeks on crude).
findings.quote: If the news was bullish, but the analyst had already predicted that, and the market had already made gains up until the announcement, then we could see a quick selloff.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 4 Event-Based Trading Examples pp. 80-88
findings.notes: For crypto: funding-rate/positioning extremes plus consensus macro narrative before CPI/FOMC. Inversion signal = pre-event run-up magnitude relative to consensus. Would need a scheduled-event + funding/positioning feature set (time, flow groups).
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Stop-loss failure taxonomy (whipsaw, slippage, fundamental shift) and ATR-based stop distance
findings.mechanism: A stop converts to a market order on trigger, so it fills at the worst price in fast markets (slippage), gets whipsawed by tight placement in consolidation, and sits too far to survive fundamental supply/demand shifts
findings.setup_summary: Classify every stop-based exit into one of three failure modes: (1) fast-moving market - triggered stop becomes market order and fills with slippage; (2) consolidating market - stop too tight is hit then price resumes expected direction (whipsaw); (3) fundamental shift - stop placed wide to survive consolidation is blown through with oversized loss. Cited countermeasure: place stops at about 1.5x true range to avoid whipsaw.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not applicable - risk-design taxonomy.
findings.risk_geometry: Stop distance floor ~1.5x true range (ATR) to reduce whipsaw; acknowledge slippage/gap risk inherent in stop-to-market conversion; stop and protective-exit are different exits (reactive vs proactive).
findings.quote: Stops are not a risk management tool; they are a panic button to help you out when all else fails.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 6 pp. 103-106; stop wisdom list p. 104
findings.notes: Maps to V8's stop (RiskGate) vs dead-thesis/still_valid (lifecycle) distinction - the book's reactive-vs-proactive split is the same line V8 draws. Encode a stop-distance floor in risk_geometry and keep stop-to-market slippage realistic in src/v8/simulator.py; 24/7 perps have no daily gaps but liquidation cascades create gap-like jumps.
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Protective-option hard stop with 50% premium-loss cap and delta-limited hedge coverage
findings.mechanism: A purchased protective option replaces the market-conversion risk of a stop with a fixed-maximum-loss instrument, but the hedge's premium erosion must be capped (50% rule) and its coverage is delta-limited (~0.80) so it is not a perfect substitute
findings.setup_summary: Instead of a stop loss, buy a protective option with a strike at a fixed % loss level (2%/5%/10% of account); the position's maximum loss is bounded by premium plus strike gap, immune to slippage, whipsaw, and gaps. Rule: never let the protective option erode more than 50% of its premium; recognize the hedge covers only ~delta cents per dollar of the adverse underlying move.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not applicable - risk-structure design.
findings.risk_geometry: Protective strike at ~2-10% loss threshold; erosion cap 50% of premium; delta caps protection (~0.80 even deep in-the-money); leg-out of the losing side converts the protective leg into the new primary position.
findings.quote: The general rule of thumb mentioned in Winning the Trading Game is not to allow a loss of greater than 50 percent of your premium.
findings.notes: No options on crypto perps, so the vehicle is DEFER_GATED. The transferable lessons for V8: (a) imperfect-hedge delta limits, (b) a hard 50% erosion cap on any protective component, and (c) the 'leg out' concept - convert the losing side into the winning side rather than stop-and-chase, which maps to V8 episode management (lifecycle_rule candidate).
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Collar: bounded-risk structure that sells premium to fund protection and lock in profits
findings.mechanism: Selling a far OTM option collects premium that offsets the protective option's cost, bounding both loss and profit to a range computable at inception
findings.setup_summary: Long collar: long underlying + buy put near support + sell call near resistance (mirror for short collar). Max profit and max loss are computable at inception; used at trade inception or to lock in profits on a winning trend by rolling the hedge forward. Rules cited: collected premium should be at least ~1/3 of the protective option's potential loss, and the trade should target a 1:2 risk:reward.
findings.trigger_invalidation: If the primary directional trade never develops, the purchased option's time value erodes while you wait; monitor option value (too far vs too close OTM) and expiration vs underlying.
findings.risk_geometry: Protective option at support level; sold OTM option at resistance; profit capped at resistance, loss capped at support minus net premium; sold premium >= 1/3 of protective max loss; 1:2 risk:reward; 50% protective-erosion cap.
findings.quote: each time an option was sold the collected premium was the equivalent of at least one-third the value of the potential loss on the protective option.
findings.notes: Options structure unavailable on perps; DEFER_GATED. The perp-native analog of 'collecting premium' is funding-rate carry; the 1:2 risk:reward and 'sold premium >= 1/3 of max loss' heuristics are risk_geometry inputs (V8 trend_pullback currently uses target_r 1.0 - the book argues for ~2R). Also covers converting a winning day trade into a protected position trade.
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Backwardation/contango rotation and cash-futures basis convergence spread
findings.mechanism: When the front month moves to a premium over deferred months (backwardation) or to a discount, the spread mean-reverts as supply/demand and carrying-cost economics normalize
findings.setup_summary: Alert on a market entering backwardation (front month above deferred months): go long front / short deferred to capture narrowing. When it reverts to contango, reverse (short front / long deferred) for the widening. Also trade cash-vs-futures convergence: hold a spot position hedged with futures until the two prices converge at expiration.
findings.trigger_invalidation: If the front contract dips below the back month (discount) on a long spread, cut immediately - a widening spread loses on both sides; persistent backwardation (squeeze) without convergence fails the thesis.
findings.risk_geometry: Pair trade with discounted spread margin; profits from the price difference; exit on discount; unwind triggers new margin requirements; stop-limits recommended because spread trades can lose on both legs simultaneously.
findings.quote: Once the alert kicks in you can take advantage of the narrowing of the gap by going long the front month and selling the further out month.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 9 pp. 148-151 (backwardation), 149-150 (basis convergence), 146-148 (old crop/new crop)
findings.notes: DATA_BLOCKED in V8 until a derivatives tape (perp + quarterly futures, e.g., BTCUSD_PERP vs BTC quarterly) exists - same precedent as breakout_retest/capitulation backlog. The seasonal old-crop/new-crop leg is NONE for crypto; the backwardation/convergence legs transfer, with funding carry as the perp-native expression (2020-21 basis spikes can persist, so convergence is not guaranteed).
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Consolidation/range regime filter (sideways dominance gate on directional experts)
findings.mechanism: Markets spend most time in sideways consolidation; forcing long/short decisions inside a range produces constant reactive whipsaw, so a range regime should suppress or restructure directional entries
findings.setup_summary: Detect a sideways/consolidation regime (book claims ~80% of the time) and use it to gate directional experts: inside a range, trend-following entries are suppressed or must be range-specific (the book's straddle enters both sides on 'sideways + pending announcement'). Range extremes act as support/resistance for the straddle/strangle buy points.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Breakout of the range terminates the consolidation state and re-enables directional setups.
findings.risk_geometry: Range extremes = support/resistance; sideways + announcement is the trigger for both-sides positioning; breakout of range initiates directional entries.
findings.quote: The sideways or consolidation pattern occurs 80 percent of the time.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 4 pp. 67-68; Ch. 4 straddle criteria p. 71
findings.notes: Most directly implementable finding: a range-state feature (e.g., ATR-relative range or volatility-compression measure) in the regime filter gating trend_pullback/failed_breakout. BTC ranges frequently; this is a feature_group + REGIME_FILTER, not a new expert family.
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Predefine loss and profit exits; treat entry price as a guideline
findings.mechanism: Slippage makes the entry price unreliable, while the loss price and profit price determine the trade's economics; fixing exits first is what controls outcome
findings.setup_summary: Every trade has five required components: entry price, loss price, profit price, trend, and counter-trend; if any is missing, sit out. Loss price and profit price must be fixed in advance and are not flexible like the entry; the traditionally acceptable risk-of-loss rule is risking one to gain two.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not a setup strategy - planning methodology.
findings.risk_geometry: Loss price and profit price set in advance; entry treated as a guideline due to slippage; 1:2 risk-of-loss rule referenced throughout.
findings.quote: your entry price is the least necessary [of entry, loss, profit]. ... Knowing your potential loss exit price and your profit exit price are essential and should not be afforded the same flexibility as the entry price.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 3 pp. 56-61 (five core components pp. 58-61)
findings.notes: Confirms V8's design: risk_geometry (entry, target_r, stop_r, expiry_bars) fixed before entry, NEXT_BAR_CLOSE entry as a slippage-tolerant guideline. The 1:2 rule is a candidate target_r revision for existing experts.
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Transaction-cost drag and overtrading (day-trader failure mode)
findings.mechanism: High trade frequency turns commission/fee and spread drag into the dominant cost; gross profits fail to cover transaction costs
findings.setup_summary: Model taker/maker fees and spread on every simulated fill and verify that expert frequency keeps net-of-cost performance positive; the cited 130,000-account Taiwan study (Barber & Odean 2004) found more than 8 in 10 day traders lose and heavy day traders' gross profits do not cover transaction costs.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not a setup strategy - program-level cost gate.
findings.risk_geometry: Fee/spread drag per fill; low-cost platforms induce more trading, not lower risk - frequency must not grow because costs are cheap.
findings.quote: Heavy day traders earn gross profits, but their profits are not sufficient to cover transaction costs.
findings.notes: Reinforces keeping the Binance USDM cost model in src/v8/simulator.py and never validating an expert gross of fees; perp taker fees + funding apply on every fill, so high-frequency variants are the most exposed.
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009

findings.strategy_name: Leverage discipline: do not use maximum available leverage
findings.mechanism: High leverage converts small adverse instrument moves into account-crippling losses and nonlinearly compresses recovery capacity
findings.setup_summary: Cap effective leverage below the exchange maximum (book cites up to 50:1 futures / 500:1 forex; perps commonly 100x+). Rule-of-thumb: cut leverage in half by doubling committed capital; trade with capital you can afford to lose; the author's margin cushion rule is ~3x contract margin for futures and ~5x for spot forex.
findings.trigger_invalidation: Not applicable - standing risk rule.
findings.risk_geometry: Effective leverage cap; margin cushion multiples (3x futures / 5x forex per author); account must survive a single-trade wipeout to remain tradable.
findings.quote: These high levels of trading leverage are a leading contributor to a retail trader's rapid demise.
findings.chapter_anchor: Ch. 1 pp. 13-14, 18 (recovery math); Ch. 6 p. 108 (margin cushion rule)
findings.notes: Distinct from risk_percent_sizing: that caps per-trade risk fraction; this caps the instrument leverage multiplier itself. Feed a leverage/heat cap into RiskGate admission for src/v8/risk.py given perp leverage up to 100-125x.
findings.book: Trade Like a Pro - 15 High-Profit Trading Strategies 2009
